passages.title: Oath by the wise Quran: Muhammad is a messenger
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat are Allah's own testimony, sealed with an oath, that Muhammad ﷺ is truly His Messenger — one of the Messengers, on a straight path, carrying a revelation sent down by the Almighty, the Most Merciful, in order to warn a people whose forefathers were not warned and who are therefore heedless. The passage moves from the mysterious opening letters, to the oath by the Qur'an, to the affirmation of the Prophet's ﷺ messengership, to the source of his revelation, to the purpose for which it was sent.

## The heart of the Qur'an

Before entering the ayat themselves, both commentaries pause over what this surah *is*. Maʿqil Ibn Yasar (may Allah be pleased with him) narrates that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Surah Ya Sin is the heart of the Qur'an." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that some words of this hadith tell us that a person who recites Surah Ya Sin exclusively for the sake of Allah and the Hereafter is forgiven, and that it should be recited over the dead among us — reported by Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim and others, as cited in Rūh-ul-Maʿānī and al-Mazhari.

Why "the heart"? Imam al-Ghazzali, quoted in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, offered a beautiful reason: this surah presents the Day of Judgment and the Resurrection with particular detail and eloquence, and belief in the Hereafter is the article of faith on which the soundness of all human deeds depends. Fear of the Hereafter readies a person for good deeds and restrains him from impermissible desires and the unlawful. Just as the body's health depends on the heart, the health of one's iman (faith) depends on concern for the Hereafter — so the surah that awakens that concern is the Qur'an's heart.

Ibn Kathir opens with the same theme of virtue. Al-Hafiz Abu Yaʿla recorded from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Whoever recites Ya Sin in the night, will wake up forgiven, and whoever recites Ha Mim in which Ad-Dukhan (the Smoke) is mentioned, will wake up forgiven" — Ibn Kathir notes its chain of narration is good (jayyid). And Ibn Hibban recorded in his Sahih from Jundub bin ʿAbdullah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Whoever recites Ya Sin in the night, seeking the Face of Allah, will be forgiven." Notice the condition in the second narration: *seeking the Face of Allah*. The promise is tied to sincerity, not mechanical recitation.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds further reports: a narration of Abu Dharr al-Ghifari (may Allah be pleased with him) that reciting Surah Ya Sin near a dying person makes the ordeal of death easy on him (reported by ad-Dailami and Ibn Hibban, as cited in al-Mazhari); ʿAbdullah Ibn Zubayr's (may Allah be pleased with him) statement that whoever puts Surah Ya Sin ahead of his need finds it fulfilled; and names by which the surah has been known in various reports — ʿAzimah; Muʿimmah, a surah that universalizes its blessings in worldly life and in the Hereafter for its readers; Mudafiʿah, the one that removes misfortunes from its readers; and Qadiyah, the caretaker of needs.

## Ayah 1 — the two letters

*Yā Sīn.* What do these letters mean? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the positions honestly. The well-known view is that they belong to the "isolated letters" (al-hurūf al-muqattaʿāt) that open certain surahs, whose knowledge rests with Allah alone — Ibn Kathir likewise simply refers the reader back to his discussion at the start of Surat Al-Baqarah. But other views were held: Ibn al-ʿArabi reports from Imam Malik that Yā Sīn is one of the names of Allah, and a narration from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) says the same. Another narration holds it is a word of the Ethiopian language meaning "O human person," denoting the person of the noble Prophet ﷺ himself; and from a saying of Ibn Jubayr (may Allah be pleased with him) it is gathered that Yā Sīn is a name of the noble Prophet ﷺ. Rūh-ul-Maʿānī remarks that giving the Prophet ﷺ a name composed of these two elegant letters — Yā and Sīn — has great secrets behind it. These readings are not presented as settled fact; the sound default remains that the letters' meaning is with Allah, while the reported views are conveyed with their attribution.

This uncertainty has a practical consequence Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records: Imam Malik disliked naming a person "Yasin," because if it is a Divine Name whose exact meaning remains unknown, it might carry a meaning exclusive to Allah — like al-Khāliq (the Creator) or ar-Rāziq (the Provider-Sustainer), names no creature may bear. Yet if the word is written with a script that reads simply "Yasin," Ibn al-ʿArabi held it permissible to give that name to a human being, since the Qur'an itself says "Salāmun ʿalā Ilyāsīn" (37:130), which in some renderings (qirāʼāt) appears as "Āl Yāsīn."

## Ayat 2–4 — the oath and what it swears to

In ayah 2 Allah swears *by the Qur'an, full of wisdom* (al-Qur'ān al-hakīm). Ibn Kathir explains al-hakīm here as al-Muhkam — the perfected Book "which falsehood cannot come to from before it or behind it."

And the claim comes in ayah 3: "Truly, you are one of the Messengers." Ibn Kathir notes the address is to Muhammad ﷺ directly: *(Truly, you)* means, "O Muhammad."

Ayah 4 completes the affirmation: *on the straight path*. Ibn Kathir explains this as "following a straight methodology and religion, and an upright Law" — a dīn (religion) and law with no crookedness. He connects this to Allah's words elsewhere: "And verily, you are indeed guiding (mankind) to the straight path. The path of Allah to Whom belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is on the earth. Verily, to Allah all matters return" (42:52–53). The straight path is Allah's own path, and to Him all matters return.

## Ayah 5 — might joined to mercy

*Sent down by the Almighty (al-ʿAzīz), the Most Merciful (al-Raḥīm).* Ibn Kathir reads this as describing the path itself: "this path which you have brought is a revelation from the Lord of might Who is Most Merciful to His believing servants." The pairing of the two names is the point: the very One who is the Lord of might is Most Merciful to His believing servants, and it is from Him that this revelation descends.

## Ayah 6 — warning a heedless people

*In order that you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned, so they are heedless.* Ibn Kathir identifies "a people" as the Arabs: no warner had come to them before him ﷺ. But he immediately guards against a wrong inference: the fact that they alone are mentioned does not mean that others are excluded, just as mentioning some individuals does not mean all others are excluded. The mission of the Prophet ﷺ is universal, established — as Ibn Kathir says — by ayat and mutawātir (mass-transmitted) hadiths, such as Allah's command: "Say: O mankind! Verily, I am sent to you all as the Messenger of Allah" (7:158).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the phrase "whose forefathers were not warned" with care, because the Qur'an also says, "and there was no community without a warner having passed among them" (35:24). How do the two fit? The "fathers" here means the *nearer* ancestors of the Arabs. Since the coming of their patriarch Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and, with him, Ismaʿil (peace be upon him), no prophet had appeared *among the Arabs themselves* for several centuries. The work of calling people to the true faith with warnings and glad tidings never ceased — Divine mercy has never kept any nation or community deprived of the essential call and warning at any time or in any region — but teachings of prophets, when communicated by their deputies, do not bring about the same effect as when the prophets deliver them in person. Therefore the verse can truly say of the Arabs that no warner came to them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a telling consequence: with no prophet among them, there was no regular system of education in Arabia where people could learn and teach, which is why the Arabs came to be called al-ummiyyūn, "the unlettered ones."

The verse itself joins the two halves with a consequence: their forefathers were not warned, *so they are heedless* (fa-hum ghāfilūn). And the purpose clause — *li-tundhira*, "in order that you may warn" — states the rationale of the mission plainly: the Almighty, the Most Merciful, sends His Messenger ﷺ precisely to warn such a people.

## Reading the passage whole

Set side by side, the six ayat build steadily: the mysterious letters open the surah (ayah 1); Allah swears by the Qur'an, full of wisdom — the perfected Book which falsehood cannot come to from before it or behind it (ayah 2); the Prophet ﷺ is affirmed as truly one of the Messengers (ayah 3), on the straight path (ayah 4); the revelation he carries is sent down by the Almighty, the Most Merciful (ayah 5); and its purpose is to warn a heedless people whose forefathers were not warned (ayah 6). For the believer, the passage settles the foundation on which the rest of Surah Ya Sin will build, and it locates certainty about the Prophet ﷺ in Allah's own sworn word. And in the surah's recitation itself — in the night, seeking the Face of Allah, as the hadith in Ibn Hibban's Sahih describes — lies the door to forgiveness its virtues promise.

passages.title: Hearts sealed against warning; only the receptive heed
passages.tafsir:
After the sūrah's opening oath — that the Prophet ﷺ is truly one of the messengers, sent to warn a heedless people — ayat 7–12 explain why that warning will land so differently on different hearts. The passage divides humanity into two: those against whom Allah's word of judgement has already come true, pictured in unforgettable images of shackles and walls (ayat 7–10), and the receptive soul who follows the Reminder and fears his Lord unseen (ayah 11). It then closes with the reason both responses matter eternally: Allah will raise the dead, and every deed — and every ripple a deed leaves behind — is being written down (ayah 12).

## "The word has proved true against most of them" (ayah 7)

Ibn Kathir transmits the explanation of Ibn Jarir: the punishment has become inevitable for most of them, because Allah has decreed in the Mother of the Book — al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ, the Preserved Tablet on which Allah has written all things — that they will not believe in Allah or in His Messengers.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up how this decree and human choice fit together. Allah placed before human beings two ways — disbelief and faith, leading to Paradise and Hell — then sent prophets and Books to give substance to the call of faith, and gave people the capacity to recognise good and evil and choose. When a person refuses to think, ignores the proofs spread throughout creation, turns from the call of the prophets and never deliberates in the Book of Allah, and so commits himself to a way, Allah then assembles for him everything that carries him further along it: for the one who embraces disbelief, "the supply of things and circumstances that would increase his disbelief never runs short." So the verse means that against most of these people, *because of their choice of evil*, Allah's decisive verdict — that they are not going to believe — already stands pronounced. The seal is real and divine; but it falls on hearts that first shut themselves.

## Two pictures of a closed heart (ayat 8–9)

The Qurʼān does not leave this state abstract. Ayah 8 paints the first picture: iron collars on their necks reaching up to their chins, so that they are *muqmaḥūn* — their heads forced up and back, unable to bend. Ibn Kathir explains the image: it is like a person with a chain around his neck and his hands bound together beneath his chin, so his head is wrenched upward. Al-ʿAwfī, narrating from Ibn ʿAbbās, connected it to the ayah "And let not your hand be tied (like a miser) to your neck" (17:29): their hands are tied to their necks and cannot stretch forth to do any good deed. Mujāhid adds that their heads are raised and their hands placed over their mouths, so they are restrained from doing anything good. Notice the economy Ibn Kathir points out — the ayah mentions only the collars, but the bound hands are understood by implication.

Ayah 9 gives the second picture: a barrier (*sadd*) in front of them, a barrier behind them, and a covering cast over them, "so that they cannot see." Of the barrier before them, Mujāhid said it stands "between them and the truth"; and of the barrier behind them he said, "Between them and the truth, so they are confused." Qatādah said, "They move from one form of misguidance to another." The covering, Ibn Kathir explains, means Allah has blinded their eyes to the truth so that they cannot benefit from goodness or be guided to it. Ibn Jarīr even records that Ibn ʿAbbās used to recite the word as *fa-aʿshaynāhum*, from *al-ʿashā* — a weakness of the sight, a blindness, which is a complaint of the eye. ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam said Allah placed this barrier between them and Islam and īmān so that they will never reach it, reciting: "Truly, those against whom the Word of your Lord has been justified will not believe, even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful torment" (10:96–97), and then said, "Whoever has been prevented by Allah will never be able."

Why *two* images? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays a penetrating observation from Imam Rāzī (via Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī): there are two kinds of barriers against perception. One prevents a person from seeing even *himself*; the other prevents him from seeing his *surroundings*. The man whose neck is shackled upward cannot lower his eyes — he cannot see his own self or the state he is in, nor the road at his feet, so he cannot avoid the ditch ahead. The man walled in on every side cannot see what lies beyond — the truth may be present all around him, yet it simply does not reach him, surrounded as he is by his ignorance, hostility and doggedness. The disbeliever suffers both: blind to his own condition, and sealed off from the truth outside.

**Parable, or event?** Ikrimah reported that Abu Jahl boasted, "If I see Muhammad, I will do such and such," whereupon these ayat were revealed — and people would say, "Here is Muhammad," while he asked, "Where is he? Where is he?", unable to see him. Ibn Jarīr recorded this, and Ibn Kathir cites it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, however, notes that the majority of commentators take the verse purely as a similitude of the disbelievers' condition, and that while such incidents about Abu Jahl and others are reported in the tafsir literature (Ibn Kathir, Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī, al-Qurṭubī, Mazharī), most of these are weak narrations and the tafsir of the verse cannot rest on them. Both readings are before you, with their advocates named; on either one, the spiritual meaning stands.

## Warning that cannot help — and the one it can (ayat 10–11)

Ayah 10 draws the conclusion: "It is the same to them whether you warn them or you warn them not; they will not believe." Ibn Kathir explains: for those about whom Allah has decreed misguidance, warning will have no effect — just as the sūrah's parallel at the opening of Sūrat al-Baqarah, and as in 10:96–97 again.

Then ayah 11 turns the light around: "You can only warn him who follows the Reminder and fears the Most Gracious unseen." The Reminder (*al-Dhikr*) is the Qurʼān, and "you can only warn" means, as Ibn Kathir puts it, only the believers — those who follow it — will actually *benefit* from your warning. The second mark of the receptive heart is *khashyat al-Raḥmān bil-ghayb*: fearing the Most Gracious "in the unseen," which Ibn Kathir explains as this — even when no one sees him except Allah, he knows that Allah is watching him and sees what he does.

For such a person the Prophet ﷺ is told: "Give him glad tidings of forgiveness and a generous reward" — forgiveness of his sins, and a reward Ibn Kathir describes as vast, great and beautiful, exactly as Allah says elsewhere: "Verily, those who fear their Lord unseen, theirs will be forgiveness and a great reward" (67:12).

## "We give life to the dead" — resurrection, and revival of hearts (ayah 12)

Ayah 12 grounds everything that came before. "Verily, We give life to the dead" refers first to the Day of Resurrection. But Ibn Kathir draws out a second, hope-filled indication: Allah also gives life to the *heart* of whomever He wills among the disbelievers — those whose hearts have died in misguidance — by guiding them to the truth, just as He says after mentioning the hardness of hearts: "Know that Allah gives life to the earth after its death" (57:17). So even this passage of sealed hearts refuses despair: the same power that raises corpses can raise a dead heart.

## What is written: deeds — and their traces

"And We record that which they send before them, and their traces." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on the phrase "send before": deeds are described as *sent ahead* because a good or bad deed does not perish here in this world — it is your baggage, forwarded to your destination in the next world where you must meet it. And the "recording" is for preservation: writing leaves no room for error, forgetfulness, increase or decrease.

The word *āthār* — "traces" or "effects" — carries two explanations among the early authorities, and Ibn Kathir gives both:

**First: the legacy a deed leaves.** Allah writes not only what people did but what their deeds set in motion after them — the fruits, outcomes and consequences that keep surviving, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words. One who taught people their religion, wrote a beneficial book, or established an endowment keeps accruing reward as long as its benefit flows; one who instituted oppressive laws or corrupting practices keeps accruing sin as long as their evil endures. The Prophet ﷺ said — as recorded by Muslim from Jarīr bin ʿAbdullāh al-Bajalī, in a narration containing the story of the people of the tribe of Muḍar who came wearing woollen rags: "Whoever starts something good in Islam will have its reward, and a reward equal to that of everyone who acts on it after him, without that detracting from their reward in the slightest; and whoever starts something evil in Islam will bear its burden, and a burden equal to that of everyone who acts on it after him, without that detracting from their burden in the slightest." In the fuller version recorded by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, the Prophet ﷺ then recited this very ayah. To the same effect is the hadith in Sahih Muslim from Abu Hurayrah: "When the son of Adam dies, all his deeds come to an end except three: knowledge which is beneficial to others, a righteous child who prays for him, or ongoing charity which he leaves behind." Mujāhid, in one report, also explained "their traces" as "what they left behind of misguidance."

**Second: literal footsteps.** Mujāhid (in another report), al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said *āthār* means their footsteps — every step walked toward obedience or disobedience is counted. Qatādah put it movingly: "If Allah were to have neglected anything with regard to you, O son of Adam, He would have neglected what the wind could remove of these footsteps" — yet even the footprints the wind erases are taken into account. Hence his counsel: whoever can have his footsteps recorded in the obedience of Allah, let him do that. The Sunnah confirms it. When Banū Salamah wanted to move their homes next to the mosque, the Prophet ﷺ told them, in the hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad and also by Muslim from Jābir: "O Banū Salamah, stay where you are, and your footsteps will be recorded; stay where you are, and your footsteps will be recorded." And Imam Ahmad — with An-Nasāʼī and Ibn Mājah — records from ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAmr that when a man died in Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ said, "Would that he had died somewhere other than his birthplace," explaining that for one who dies away from where he was born, space is measured for him in Paradise from his birthplace to where his footsteps ended. The Companions lived by this: Ibn Jarīr relates that Thābit said, "I was walking with Anas and I began to walk quickly. He took my hand and we walked slowly, and when we had finished praying, Anas said, 'I walked with Zayd bin Thābit and I was walking quickly, and he said: O Anas! Do you not feel that your footsteps are being written down?'"

Ibn Kathir rules that there is no contradiction between the two explanations — rather, the footsteps reading proves the point *more* forcefully: if even literal footsteps are recorded, then deeds which set an example, good or bad, are all the more surely recorded. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses one further puzzle: this sūrah is Makkan, while the Banū Salamah incident is from Madinah. The answer it gives — crediting Ibn Kathir's preference — is that the verse was revealed in Makkah in its general sense, and when the event later occurred in Madinah, the Prophet ﷺ cited the verse in support, counting footprints among the "traces" it mentions.

## The Clear Book

The ayah ends: "and all things We have recorded with numbers in a Clear Register (Imām Mubīn)." Ibn Kathir explains — on the authority of Mujāhid, Qatādah and ʿAbdur-Raḥmān bin Zayd bin Aslam — that this is al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ, the Preserved Tablet, the source of all records, in which everything that exists is precisely set down. Ibn Kathir compares it to "the Day when We shall call together all human beings with their Imām" (17:71) — the book of deeds that will testify for or against its owner — and it is the Book of which the criminals will cry on that Day: "What sort of Book is this that leaves neither a small thing nor a big thing, but has recorded it!" (18:49), "and your Lord treats no one with injustice."

## Living it

The passage asks two things of the believer. First, guard against the shackled posture: the person in ayat 8–9 is the one who never lowers his gaze to examine himself and never lets the truth outside reach him. Self-scrutiny and openness to the Reminder are the opposite of the collar and the walls. Second, take the recording of *traces* seriously — in both directions. Every step to the mosque is written; so is every practice, good or evil, that outlives you in other people's hands. As Qatādah said, let whoever is able have his footsteps recorded in the obedience of Allah — and let him think hard about what of his deeds will still be bearing fruit, and still being written, long after he is gone.

passages.title: The parable of the town that rejected three messengers
passages.tafsir:
## A parable for those who disbelieve

This passage opens the story of an unnamed town to which Allah sent three messengers, all of whom the townspeople rejected — first with mockery of their humanity, then with superstition and open threats. What binds ayat 13–19 together is a single escalating dialogue: the messengers' calm, patient case for their mission set against the town's hardening refusal, moving from "you are only telling lies" (ayah 15) to "we will surely stone you" (ayah 18).

The passage begins with a command to the Prophet ﷺ: **"Give them an example"** (ayah 13). Ibn Kathir explains the address plainly: "Allah says, 'O Muhammad, tell your people who disbelieve in you'" — the story is told, in the first instance, for those of his own people who were disbelieving in him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the expression *ḍarb mathal* ("to cite an example") is generally used to prove something by the example of a similar thing: the event is narrated by the Qurʼān to alert people against disbelievers who rejected the very notion of there being a prophet or messenger. In other words, the town is a mirror held up to all who reject a messenger — and, as Ibn Kathir will show, everything its people say had already been said by nation after disbelieving nation.

## Which town was it?

The Qurʼān deliberately leaves the town unnamed, and the commentators discussed this at length.

**The majority view: Antioch (Antakiyah).** Ibn Ishaq reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, Kaʿb al-Ahbar and Wahb bin Munabbih that it was the city of Antioch, ruled by an idol-worshipping king called Antiochus son of Antiochus son of Antiochus; Allah sent him three messengers — named in that report Sadiq, Saduq and Shalum — and he disbelieved in them. The same identification was narrated from Buraydah bin al-Husayb, ʿIkrimah, Qatadah and az-Zuhri. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the majority of commentators opted for this, that Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir said no counter-statement is reported from any commentator, and that Yaqut al-Hamawi (author of Muʿjam ul-Buldan) records the grave of Habib Najjar — whose story comes a little later — as a known site in Antakiyah, visited by people from far and near.

**Ibn Kathir's hesitation.** Yet Ibn Kathir himself, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates, was reluctant to accept this. His reasons: Antioch was one of the four great centres of the Christian faith (with Jerusalem, Rome and Alexandria) and the *first* city to embrace the faith of ʿIsa عليه السلام — whereas the town of this passage was a town of disbelievers and, by the Qurʼān's explicit account, was destroyed by a punishment that left no one alive. History records no such annihilation of the famous Antioch. So, he reasoned, either it is a different town altogether, or another town that happened to bear the same name.

**The wisest resolution.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Maulana Ashraf Thanavi in Bayan-ul-Qurʼan: understanding these verses does not depend on locating the town at all. Since the Qurʼān kept it ambiguous, there is no need to labour to fix it — as the early Muslims' famous maxim puts it, "Leave ambiguous that which Allah has left ambiguous." The lesson, not the geography, is the point.

## Three messengers — prophets, or disciples of ʿIsa?

Ayah 14 gives the sequence: two messengers were sent first, the town denied them both, so Allah "reinforced them with a third" — the word *ʿazzaznā* meaning, as Ibn Kathir explains, "We supported and strengthened them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the picture: first two came and were refused a hearing; then Allah strengthened them with a third; then all three together addressed the town.

Who were they? The scholars genuinely differed, and both commentaries lay out the two views:

- **They were prophets of Allah.** In the Qurʼān the words *rasūl* and *mursal* are generally used for a prophet, and here Allah attributes their sending directly to Himself ("When *We* sent to them…"), which indicates prophethood. This is the report of Ibn Ishaq from Ibn ʿAbbas, Kaʿb al-Ahbar and Wahb bin Munabbih. Ibn Kathir preferred this view, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the apparent sense of the Qurʼān's wording also supports it.
- **They were disciples of ʿIsa عليه السلام.** Qatadah held that *mursalūn* here is not used in its technical sense of prophets but simply means "bearers of a message": the three were from among the disciples of ʿIsa, sent to the town on his order. Since ʿIsa was himself Allah's messenger, his sending them was indirectly Allah's sending, which is why it is attributed to Allah. Al-Qurtubi and others adopted this view.

As for their names, the reports differ — Sadiq, Saduq and Shalum in one narration; in another, transmitted by Ibn Jurayj from Wahb bin Sulayman from Shuʿayb al-Jabaʼi, the first two were Shamʿun and Yuhanna and the third Bulus. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes the question as the sources do: *Allah knows best.*

## "You are only humans like us" — the oldest objection

In ayah 15 the townspeople raise the objection that runs through the whole history of disbelief: "You are only human beings like ourselves, and the Most Gracious has revealed nothing. You are only telling lies." Ibn Kathir unpacks the logic: 'how could you receive revelation when you are human and we are human — why do we not receive revelation like you? If you were really messengers, you would be angels.'

Ibn Kathir then shows this is not one town's quirk but the signature argument of every rejecting nation, citing a chain of parallel ayat: "Shall mere men guide us?" (64:6); "You are no more than human beings like us! You wish to turn us away from what our fathers used to worship" (14:10); "If you were to obey a human being like yourselves, then verily, you indeed would be losers" (23:34); and "Nothing prevented men from believing when the guidance came to them, except that they said: 'Has Allah sent a man as (His) Messenger?'" (17:94). The parable's force — for the people it first addressed and for every later reader — lies exactly here: this objection to a messenger's humanity was nothing new; it was the refrain of nation after nation that denied its messengers.

## The messengers' answer: Allah as witness, conveying as duty

The reply in ayat 16–17 is striking for what it does *not* do. The messengers do not trade insults; they appeal to Allah's knowledge: "Our Lord knows that we have truly been sent to you." Ibn Kathir explains the weight packed into that sentence: Allah knows we are His messengers — if we were lying, He would have taken the utmost vengeance against us; but He will cause us to prevail, and you will come to know whose end is the happy one in the Hereafter. He compares it to the ayah, "Say: Sufficient is Allah for a witness between me and you…" (29:52). To make Allah your witness is the ultimate oath of a truthful claimant — because the One invoked has full power to expose and punish the liar.

Then ayah 17: "And our duty is only to deliver the message clearly" — *al-balāgh al-mubīn*, the plain conveying. Ibn Kathir: 'all we have to do is convey the Message with which we have been sent; if you obey, happiness will be yours in this world and the Hereafter, and if you do not respond, you will soon know the consequences.' The messenger's responsibility ends at clear delivery; the results belong to Allah. It is a definition of the prophetic task itself — and, by extension, of everyone who calls to Allah.

## "We see you as a bad omen" — superstition turned to threat

With argument exhausted, the town turns in ayah 18 to superstition and violence: "We definitely see you as a bad omen… if you do not cease, we will surely stone you, and a painful torment will touch you from us." The word here, *taṭayyur*, means (as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains) seeing an evil omen in someone, treating a person as a carrier of misfortune. Ibn Kathir records the early explanations: Qatadah said they meant "if something bad befalls us, it will be because of you," and Mujahid said they claimed, "People like you never enter a town but its people are punished." On the threat itself, Qatadah explained *lanarjumannakum* concretely: "by throwing stones at you."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a detail found in some narrations: a famine had overtaken the town after its people curtly turned down the messengers' good counsel — and, in the common habit of disbelievers, they hastened to blame the very people who were their guides and benefactors. Both commentaries note how precisely this repeats earlier history: Firʿawn's people ascribed every evil to Musa and those with him (7:131), and the people of Salih told him, "We augur ill omen from you and those with you" (27:47).

## "Your bad omen lies within yourselves"

The messengers' final answer in ayah 19 turns the accusation back on its makers: *ṭāʼirukum maʿakum* — "your evil omen is with you." Ibn Kathir explains: the omens 'are thrown back at you.' Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word *ṭāʼir* essentially denotes bad omen or misfortune, and at times the *effects* of misfortune — wretchedness itself; that is the sense here (as in Ibn Kathir and Qurtubi). The misfortune afflicting the town was not radiating from the messengers; it was the fruit of the people's own state.

Then the piercing question: "Is it because you are admonished?" — followed by the verdict, "Rather, you are a transgressing people" (*qawmun musrifūn*). Qatadah captures the messengers' meaning: "Because we reminded you about Allah, you saw an evil omen in us. Nay, but you are a mischievous people." Ibn Kathir spells it out: 'because we admonished you and told you to worship Allah Alone and with all sincerity, in return you said what you said and threatened us.' Their crime was answering a reminder with menace — the mark of a people who have crossed all bounds.

## Living the passage

In the translation of Ibn Kathir's tafsir, this story is presented under the heading "a lesson that those who belied their Messengers were destroyed," and its living relevance follows the shape of the dialogue itself. The caller to Allah learns the messengers' posture: state the truth, take Allah as witness, and know that the duty is *clear conveying* — not forcing results. And the passage exposes two reflexes of the rejecting heart that a believer must guard against: dismissing truth because its bearer is an ordinary human being, and blaming one's misfortunes on the very people who give sincere counsel. The Qurʼān's answer to the second stands for all time: your omen — your wretchedness — is with you, in your own deeds.

passages.title: The believer from the city's edge and his reward
passages.tafsir:
# The Believer from the City's Edge (Ya-Sin 36:20–27)

This passage is the turning point of the story of the town to whom Allah sent three messengers. Just as the people resolve to reject — and even kill — those messengers, a single ordinary man comes hurrying in from the outskirts, pleads with his people to believe, declares his own faith, is killed for it, and is welcomed into Paradise. What binds these eight ayat together is one man's journey: from the edge of the city to the centre of its crisis, and from martyrdom straight into honour with Allah. His speech occupies ayat 20–25; his reward, ayat 26–27.

## Who was this man?

The Qur'an itself deliberately leaves him unnamed — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Qur'an "has left this too as ambiguous," mentioning neither his name nor who he was. This is a recurring feature of the surah's story: the lesson matters more than the identities. But the historical reports fill in a moving portrait. Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Ishaq — quoting what reached him from Ibn 'Abbas, Ka'b al-Ahbar and Wahb ibn Munabbih — that when the people of the city resolved to kill their messengers, this man came running "to help them against his people." His name was Habib; one report says he worked with ropes, while Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the most famous view is that he was a carpenter. He was a sickly man who suffered from leprosy, yet remarkably charitable — giving half of his earnings in charity — and his *fitrah*, his natural inclination, was sound. Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of 'Ikrimah, named him Habib an-Najjar and confirmed that he was killed by his people.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds fuller background from the historical narrations: he had originally been an idolater. In the report of Wahb ibn Munabbih, he lived at the farthest gate of the city and had prayed to his idols for seventy years to be cured of his leprosy — and nothing happened. When the messengers entered the city through that very gate, he challenged them: how could their Lord change in a day what seventy years of prayer to his gods had not? They replied that their Lord is powerful over everything, while his gods have no reality — they can neither benefit nor harm anyone. They prayed for him, Allah healed him completely, his faith became firm, and he pledged half his daily earnings in Allah's way. Other narrations say he then retired to a cave to devote himself to worship. When news reached him that the city had turned hostile and was threatening to kill the messengers, he came — moved, Maʿārif says, by two concerns at once: the good of his own people and the safety of the messengers.

## The language of ayah 20

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out two points from the wording. First, earlier in the story (ayah 13) the place was called *al-qaryah*, which in Arabic usage means simply a habitation, small or large; here it is called *al-madinah*, a word used only for a big city — a detail supporting the reports that this was a major city, identified in the narrations as Antakiyah (Antioch). Second, the word *yasʿā* ("rushing") comes from a root meaning to move at a running gait — but it is also used for walking with concern, poise and a sense of purpose, as in Surah al-Jumuʿah's command to "hasten to the remembrance of Allah" (62:9). Maʿārif holds that this purposeful, urgent sense is what is intended here: not panic, but a man moving with everything at stake. And he comes from *aqsā al-madinah* — the farthest outskirts. Faith had not yet reached the city's heart, but it had reached its edge, and the man of the edge came running to the centre.

## His argument (ayat 20–25)

His speech is a compact masterpiece of sincere preaching, and Ibn Kathir unpacks it phrase by phrase.

**"O my people, obey the messengers… obey those who ask no wages of you, and who are rightly guided" (20–21).** He gives his people two tests any honest mind can apply: these men want nothing from you for the message they convey, and what they call to — the worship of Allah alone, with no partner — is right guidance. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān expands the first point beautifully: here are men who travelled far, bearing the hardships of the road, asking nothing in return. Selflessness itself is evidence; it invites an honest person to stop and think.

**"And why should I not worship Him Who created me, and to Whom you shall be returned" (22).** Ibn Kathir explains: what could possibly stop me from sincerely worshipping the One who originated me? And the return — *"to Him you shall be returned"* — is the Day of Resurrection, when He will requite every deed, good with reward and evil with punishment. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to a deliberate wisdom in the wording of his warning: Habib an-Najjar did not attribute the error directly to his people; he gave it the form of attributing it to himself — as if to say, "if *I* were to do so, it would really be a grave error" — asking, "And what excuse do I have if I do not worship the One who has created me?" He said it this way so that the adversary would not be enraged, but would think about it with a cool mind.

**"Shall I take besides Him gods?" (23).** Ibn Kathir calls this a rhetorical question intended to rebuke and chastise. The man then states the decisive argument against idolatry: if ar-Rahman — the Most Gracious — intends me any harm, the intercession of these gods will be of no use to me whatsoever, nor can they save me. His point, as Ibn Kathir puts it, is that these objects of worship possess no power whatsoever — they can neither harm nor benefit, and they cannot save anyone from what Allah has willed, for "none can remove it but He" (6:17).

**"Then I would truly be in plain error" (24)** — that is, Ibn Kathir explains, *if* I were to take them as gods instead of Allah. Then the declaration that seals his fate: **"Verily, I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me!" (25).**

Who is he addressing in ayah 25? Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān record two readings. He may be addressing his own people — "I have believed in your Lord," the Lord they denied but Who is in reality their Lord — telling them: listen to what I say. Or he may be turning to the messengers themselves: "I have believed in your Lord Who sent you — so listen to what I say, and bear witness to it before my Lord, that I have believed in your Lord and followed you." Ibn Jarir judged this second interpretation "more apparent, and Allah knows best."

## His death

Ibn Ishaq reports, from what reached him from Ibn 'Abbas, Ka'b and Wahb: "When he said that, they turned on him as one, and killed him at once, and he had no one to protect him from that." Qatadah said they stoned him, and even as they did, he kept saying, *"O Allah, guide my people, for they do not know"* — they kept stoning him until he died a violent death, still praying for his killers. Muhammad ibn Ishaq also reported, from some of his companions from Ibn Mas'ud, that they stamped on him until his intestines came out. He entered the story pleading for his people's guidance and left it the same way.

## "Enter Paradise" (ayat 26–27)

The Qur'an does not even pause over his death — the very next word is his welcome: **"It was said: Enter Paradise."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the words "Enter Paradise" are themselves the hint that he was martyred, since perceiving Paradise comes only after death; the address was communicated through an angel. Maʿārif, citing Qurtubi, explains what this entry means: essentially, the glad news that his place in Paradise is settled, to be fully realised after the Resurrection — though it is not remote that he was actually shown his place then and there, and in the intermediate state after death known as *barzakh*, those bound for Paradise are already given comfort and provision from it, a virtual entry into Paradise. Ibn Kathir adds Mujahid's comment: "It was said to Habib an-Najjar, 'Enter Paradise.' This was his right, for he had been killed" — and Allah took from him all the sickness, grief and exhaustion of this world.

Then comes one of the most tender moments in the Qur'an. Seeing his reward, he says: **"Would that my people knew that my Lord has forgiven me and made me of the honoured ones!"** His first thought in Paradise is the very people who killed him. Qatadah drew the lesson: "You will never find a believer but he is sincere and is never insincere." Ibn 'Abbas said: "He was sincere towards his people during his lifetime by saying, 'O my people, obey the messengers,' and after his death by saying, 'Would that my people knew that my Lord has forgiven me and made me of the honoured ones.'" Abu Mijlaz explained the cause of the honour: "Because of my faith in my Lord and my belief in the messengers." As Ibn Kathir puts it, he wished his people could see the everlasting blessings he had attained, so that this would lead them to follow the messengers — "may Allah have mercy on him and be pleased with him, for he was so keen that his people should be guided."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records, among the historical narratives, a report from Ibn 'Abbas and the early tafsir authorities Muqatil and Mujahid: that this man was Habib ibn Isma'il an-Najjar, and that he is among those who believed in our noble Prophet ﷺ six hundred years before he actually appeared — just as it has been reported of the great tubbaʿ (the line of kings in Yemen) that he came to believe in him long before his birth by reading the prophecies of his coming in the past scriptures, and as the third such elder, Waraqah ibn Nawfal, believed in him before he was ordained and gave his call as prophet; Waraqah is mentioned in the hadith of Sahih al-Bukhari as part of the events relating to the first descent of revelation. Maʿārif notes this as a singularity of the Holy Prophet ﷺ: these three had believed in him before his birth and ordainment, something that came to pass for no other messenger or prophet.

## Was the city Antioch?

Many of the Salaf identified the city as Antioch and the three messengers as envoys of the Messiah 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon him, as Qatadah stated. But Ibn Kathir raises three careful objections: the Qur'an's plain wording presents these men as messengers from Allah Himself ("When *We* sent to them two messengers…"); historically, Antioch was the first city whose people believed in the Messiah, whereas this city rejected its messengers and was destroyed; and the Salaf, including Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, held that after the Tawrah was revealed Allah did not annihilate whole nations by heavenly punishment. So, Ibn Kathir concludes, either it was a different city, or another Antioch than the famous one — and Allah knows best. The Qur'an's silence on the name is itself instructive: the lesson does not depend on geography.

## Living it: the prophetic method of calling to Allah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes this passage with guidance it says is "worth repeated consideration" for anyone who conveys Islam. Compare what was said to the messengers and Habib — "you are only humans like us," "you are plain liars," threats of stoning — with how they answered: no anger, no cursing, only "Our Lord knows that we have been sent to you" and "our duty is only to convey clearly." Habib himself appealed to reason gently, put the argument in the first person to spare his hearers' pride, prayed for his killers as they killed him, and longed for their guidance even from Paradise. Maʿārif observes that this selfless love for Allah's creatures, even when treated unjustly, "is one thing that has changed the destinies of nations" — and laments that preachers who trade in anger and wounding remarks only harden their audiences. The believer from the city's edge shows the alternative: urgency in coming, gentleness in speaking, steadfastness in dying, and goodwill that not even martyrdom could extinguish.

passages.title: One blast destroys the town; lament over heedless peoples
passages.tafsir:
## One Cry, and a City Falls Silent

This passage closes the story of the town to whom the messengers were sent. The believing man of the city has just been martyred and welcomed into Paradise; now the camera turns back to the people he left behind. Ayat 28–29 describe their destruction — no armies, no drawn-out siege, just a single Cry — and ayat 30–32 pull back from this one town to lament the whole pattern of human history: every messenger mocked, generation after generation destroyed, and all of them, without exception, to be gathered before Allah. What holds the passage together is a single contrast: how easily Allah ends a heedless people, and how heavy the regret will be when they finally see the truth.

## Why no army? (Ayah 28)

Ayah 28 says something at first surprising: "We did not send any soldiers from the heavens against his people." Why mention what Allah did *not* do?

Ibn Kathir explains that after this people had disbelieved the Messengers and killed Allah's close friend — the believing man of the city — Allah took revenge on them. But He did not send an army of angels, "nor did He need to send them, to destroy these people; the matter was simpler than that." This was the view of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, according to the reports of Ibn Ishaq from some of his companions, and he put it memorably: "We did not seek to outnumber them, for the matter was simpler than that."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the same point: it was never the way of Allah to send an army of angels against a rebellious nation, because a single angel of Allah is enough to destroy the greatest, mightiest and bravest of nations. Why would He need to send an army of angels? The verse denies the army precisely to display the effortlessness of divine power — the destruction of a whole city did not even rise to the level of a military operation.

Ibn Kathir also records a second reading, from Mujahid and Qatadah: that what Allah did not send down after the man's death was *another Message* — Qatadah said, "Allah did not rebuke his people after they killed him." On this reading, the door of revelation simply closed on them; there was nothing left but the punishment. Ibn Jarir preferred the first view, reasoning that "the Message does not need to be brought by an army" — the wording about soldiers fits punishment, not revelation. Both readings converge on the same terrifying quiet: after the martyr fell, heaven sent them nothing more.

## The Şayḥah — a single Cry (Ayah 29)

"All it took was one blast, and they were extinguished." The Arabic word is *ṣayḥah* — a Cry, a shout, a blast of sound. Ibn Kathir relates from the scholars of Tafsir that Allah sent Jibril, peace be upon him, who seized the pillars at the gate of their city and hurled one Cry upon them — "and lo! they (all) were still, to the last man among them, and no soul was left in any body." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise reports from hadith narrations that Jibraʼil al-Amin, holding the two sides of the city gate, gave a hard and horrendous Cry whose shock no living soul could bear, and they all succumbed to sudden death. Ibn Kathir also records, from the report of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that Allah destroyed that tyrant king and the people of the city so completely that "they disappeared from the face of the earth, leaving no trace behind."

The word the Qur'an chooses for their end repays attention. **Khāmidūn** comes from *khamada* / *khumūd*, words used in Arabic for the dying down or extinguishing of a fire. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the image: the life of the living depends on energy; when that energy is gone, what remains is death. So *khāmidūn* means extinguished, put out, gone extinct — a whole city snuffed like a flame. One breath of sound from one angel, and every hearth of life in the town went cold. Set this against the martyr in the previous ayat, who at the very same moment was entering Paradise with all its bountiful provision: two deaths in one story, one an extinguishing, the other an honouring.

**Was this Antioch?** Many of the Salaf, including Qatadah, said the city was Antioch and the three Messengers were envoys sent by the Messiah ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, peace be upon him. Ibn Kathir respectfully questions this identification on three grounds. First, the Qur'an's own wording — "When *We* sent to them two Messengers… We reinforced them with a third" — presents them as Messengers from Allah Himself; had they been Disciples of the Messiah, they would surely have said something to indicate they came from him, and the people's objection "You are only human beings like ourselves" fits deniers of prophethood, not of an apostle's delegation. Second, history records that Antioch *believed* — it was the first city to accept the Messiah, and one of the four cities in which there are Christian patriarchs — whereas the Qur'an says this town rejected the Messengers and was destroyed. Third, Abu Sa'id Al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, and others among the Salaf held that after the Tawrah was revealed Allah no longer destroyed entire nations by a punishment from heaven, but instead commanded the believers to fight — citing "And indeed We gave Musa – after We had destroyed the generations of old – the Scripture" (28:43); yet the Antioch story would fall after the Tawrah. So Ibn Kathir concludes the town was likely a different city, or, if the name is kept, another Antioch than the famous one — and each time he adds, "And Allah knows best." The lesson does not hang on the map reference.

## "Alas for mankind!" (Ayah 30)

With ayah 30 the passage suddenly widens. *Yā ḥasratan ʿalā al-ʿibād* — "Oh pity, such beings!" — is a cry of lament over the servants of Allah as a whole, not just this one town. Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by Ali bin Abi Talhah, explained it as: woe to mankind. Qatadah said: "Alas for mankind, who have neglected the command of Allah."

Ibn Kathir explains what the lament points to: on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the punishment with their own eyes, they will feel regret and sorrow over how they disbelieved the Messengers of Allah and went against His commands in this world — regret that arrives only when the punishment is already before their eyes.

And the reason for the lament is given in the same breath: "No messenger ever came to them without their mocking him." Not this town only — *no* messenger, *ever*. Ibn Kathir comments: they disbelieved him, made fun of him, and rejected the message of truth with which he had been sent. Mockery is the signature response of heedlessness; it lets a people dismiss the truth without ever having to weigh it.

## They will not return — but they will be brought (Ayat 31–32)

Ayah 31 asks the deniers a question meant to sting: "Have they not considered how many peoples We destroyed before them?" — and then adds the clause that carries the theology: "they will not return to them." Ibn Kathir reads this as a refutation of the belief in the transmigration of souls — reincarnation. Some people claimed, in the words of the Qur'an elsewhere, "There is nothing but our life of this world! We die and we live!" (23:37) — the belief, in their ignorance, that they would come back to this world as they had been before. Allah refuted their false belief: the destroyed generations came to this world only once, and will not return to it. The past nations are not circling back; they are gone from this world for good — which is exactly why their ruins should be read as a lesson, not as scenery.

But "they will not return" is not the end of their story. Ayah 32 completes it: "Yet they will all be brought before Us." Ibn Kathir explains: all of the past nations, and those yet to come, will be gathered and brought to account before Allah on the Day of Judgement, and repaid according to their good and evil deeds — as Allah says elsewhere, "And verily, to each of them your Lord will repay their works in full" (11:111). Notice the two directions of the passage's ending. No one returns *here*; everyone is brought *there*. The word *muḥḍarūn* — "brought before Us" — pictures a summons no one declines. History's silence over the destroyed towns is not the final verdict; the final verdict waits at the gathering.

## Living it

The passage asks one thing above all: do not be the people who only understand when understanding no longer helps. The town heard three Messengers and a sincere man from among themselves, and answered with mockery and murder; heaven's reply took a single moment. The believing man wished — even from Paradise — that his people could know what he now knew, "so keen," as Ibn Kathir says, "that his people should be guided." The listener still in this life holds the one advantage those generations lost: the chance to take the lesson from the ruins of others rather than becoming a ruin from which others take a lesson. And whatever this world does or does not settle, ayah 32 stands: all of us, everyone, will be brought before Allah.

passages.title: Signs in the revived earth and created pairs
passages.tafsir:
This passage turns the reader's eyes to the ground under his feet: earth that was dead, then alive; bare, then heavy with grain, date palms, grapes, and running springs. What binds ayat 33–36 together is a single argument made twice over — the same scene is at once **proof** of Allah's power to raise the dead, and a **favour** that demands gratitude. Ibn Kathir heads the whole section "Proof of the Creator of the Universe and of Life after Death," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that most of the subjects taken up in Sūrah Yā Sīn relate to signs of Divine power and the rewards and favours bestowed on human beings, and that these signs do double duty: "clear proofs of His perfect power" on one hand, and "mirrors of particular rewards and favors of Allah Taʿālā" on the other.

## The dead earth as an everyday resurrection

In ayah 33, Allah calls the dead land "a sign for them" — in Ibn Kathir's words, "evidence for them of the existence of the Creator and His perfect power and ability to resurrect the dead." The scene is deliberately ordinary. The land lies "dead and arid, with no vegetation"; then Allah sends water upon it, and "it is stirred (to life), and it swells and puts forth every lovely kind (of growth)." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the point that this is not a hidden or exotic proof: the land "is there, all the time, before everyone," and it is "physically seen" that rain revives it, "so to say," making it live again. Everyone can watch this; no special learning is needed. The argument for resurrection is thus placed where no one can claim they never saw it — if Allah visibly gives life to dead earth, the raising of the dead on the Day of Judgment is no strange claim. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this is exactly why the sūrah gathers these signs: to establish "that there is a life hereafter and that people need to be firm in their belief in being raised again."

Notice how the sign unfolds in stages across ayat 33–34. First the bare essential: grain — "We bring forth from it grains, so that they eat thereof," which Ibn Kathir glosses as "a provision for them and their cattle." Then delight beyond necessity: gardens of date palms and grapes. Then the hidden machinery that sustains it all: springs made to gush forth, which Ibn Kathir describes as rivers Allah "created therein… which flow to the places where they are needed." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān widens the frame further: winds, clouds, and land — "the entire range of the natural forces" — have all been harnessed for one stated purpose in ayah 35, "so that they may eat fruits thereof."

## "And their hands made it not" — two readings, both true

The heart of ayah 35 is the small phrase *wa mā ʿamilathu aydīhim*, and the classical commentators read the particle **mā** in two ways. Both readings are recorded in the sources, and each yields a lesson.

**The majority reading — mā as negation:** "their hands made it *not*." This was the view of Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah, as Ibn Kathir reports: all of this "could only come about by the mercy of Allah towards them, not by their own efforts and labor and strength." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān hears in this a warning aimed at heedless man, and spells it out concretely: yes, you put the seed in the land, you water it, you keep the soil soft so the delicate buds can sprout. "But, making a whole tree grow from that tiny seed, having leaves and branches shoot out from it and then commission it to produce all sorts of fruits is something totally different. What is your contribution in all these things?" That, it says, is "the unshared domain of the one who is absolutely powerful, wise and knowing" — something no human hand can do. It cites the parallel in Sūrah al-Wāqiʿah (56:63–64): "Well, tell Me about that (seed) which you sow: Is it you who grow it, or are We the One who grows?" The farmer's labour is real, but it is preparation, not creation.

**Ibn Jarir's reading — mā as a relative pronoun** (*alladhī*, "that which"): they eat of its fruit *and of what their hands have made*. On this reading the ayah counts a second blessing on top of the first: not only the raw fruit Allah creates, but everything human skill then makes from it. Ibn Kathir notes that Ibn Jarir mentioned other possible interpretations but favoured this one, and that it fits the recitation of Ibn Masʿūd, which reads *wa mimmā ʿamilathu aydīhim* — "and *from* what their own hands have done." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān develops it beautifully: desserts made from fruit, chutneys and pickles, oils pressed from fruits — Allah first makes the fruit edible "without any functional human input," and then gives man "the ingenuity to prepare all sorts of delicious and useful things from each single kind of fruit." It even draws out a distinction between man and animal here: animals "all feed on simples" — the grass-eater eats only grass, the meat-eater only meat — while combining ingredients, seasoning, and cooking into countless dishes "happens to be the singularity of human beings alone," a culinary art Allah Himself taught. So even the pickle jar on the shelf turns out to be a divine gift twice over: the fruit, and the skill.

On either reading, the ayah lands on the same question: *afalā yashkurūn* — "Will they not then give thanks?" Ibn Kathir: will they not give thanks "for the innumerable blessings that He has bestowed upon them"? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sharpens it: after seeing all this, "how is it possible from a reasonable person that he does not be grateful to Allah?" Ingratitude here is not merely a moral lapse; it is unreasonable.

## Ayah 36: glory to the Creator of all the pairs

The passage closes by lifting from the field and orchard to the whole of creation. *Subḥāna alladhī khalaqa al-azwāja kullahā* — "Glory be to Him Who has created all the pairs," or in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's rendering, "Pure is the One who has created all the pairs." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān marks the transition: after land produce and climate, human beings and animals are brought into the picture, "whereby there appears yet another sign of the absolute Power." The word **azwāj** is the plural of *zawj*: as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, a pair is "two things of the same kind," each the match or counterpart of the other — a husband and wife are each the *zawj* of the other, and so with the males and females of animals.

The ayah names three domains. First, **what the earth produces**: Ibn Kathir says crops, fruits, and plants; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that pairing runs through the plant kingdom itself — many trees have male and female, with date palms and papaya as familiar examples, and modern scientific information has identified procreation in fruit- and flower-bearing trees generally. Second, **of themselves**: Ibn Kathir — "He made them into male and female." Third, **that which they know not**: in Ibn Kathir's words, "different kinds of creatures of which they know nothing," which he links to the ayah "And of everything We have created pairs, that you may remember" (51:49). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that it is not improbable that the same male-and-female arrangement exists even in solids, minerals, and other elements of creation "in a manner not discovered as yet" — precisely what "that which they do not know" leaves room for. Allah alone knows how many kinds of living forms, vegetation, and minerals lie under the layers of the earth, in the rivers, and in the mountains.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records a broader sense given by the commentators generally: *azwāj* can mean categories and kinds, since contrasting things are also called pairs — chill and heat, land and water, sorrow and happiness, health and sickness — each with its further degrees, and likewise the many kinds among humans and animals in colour, form, language, and way of life. On this reading the ayah glorifies Allah as the Creator of the entire variegated order of things.

## Living it

The passage is gentle but pointed. It does not ask the believer to abandon farming, cooking, or craft — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says plainly that "human beings are duty-bound to derive benefit out of these things." What it forbids is the forgetfulness that mistakes preparation for creation: "they should never forget the Creator and master of whatever there is." Two habits follow directly from these ayat. When rain falls on dry ground and it greens, see in it a rehearsal of resurrection — the very proof Allah chose to set "before everyone." And when food reaches your hand — the grain, the fruit, and every dish human skill has made of them — answer the question the ayah leaves hanging: *afalā yashkurūn?* Give thanks, and say with the ayah: glory be to Him Who created all the pairs.

passages.title: Signs in the night, sun, moon, and their orbits
passages.tafsir:
This passage places three cosmic signs before the reader: the night from which the day is stripped away (ayah 37), the sun running its appointed course (ayah 38), and the moon passing through its measured stages (ayah 39) — then seals them with a statement of perfect, collision-free order (ayah 40). It continues the argument begun at ayah 33, where the land, given life so that grain was brought forth from it, was "a sign for them": having described the signs of Divine power in what was created on the earth, the text now turns to the cosmic creations. Ibn Kathir names the theme plainly: these are "among the signs of the might and power of Allah" — further proof of His great might and power, from the One who is al-ʿAzīz, the Almighty, and al-ʿAlīm, the All-Knowing.

## Ayah 37 — the day "skinned" from the night

The verse says of the night, *naslakhu minhu al-nahār* — "We strip the day from it." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on the verb: **salkh** literally means *to skin an animal*. When a hide is peeled away, what was underneath becomes visible. The similitude teaches something startling: in this world, **darkness is the underlying reality and light is the covering laid over it**. Daylight is transitory — spread over the earth's darkness — and in a predetermined system, at a fixed time, that covering is peeled off from above. What remains, exposed, is the darkness we call night. Hence the suddenness of *fa-idhā hum muẓlimūn* — "and behold, they are in darkness."

Ibn Kathir reads the same verse in terms of the ceaseless alternation Allah describes elsewhere: "He brings the night as a cover over the day, seeking it rapidly" (7:54). One comes and the other goes, on and on, never failing. And he notes that this plain, observable meaning of nightfall — "the apparent meaning of the ayah" — is what the hadith works with: "When the night comes from here, and the day departs from here, and the sun has set, then the fasting person should break his fast." The great cosmic transition is, at the same time, the humble signal by which an ordinary believer knows his iftar has come.

## Ayah 38 — the sun and its mustaqarr

"And the sun runs (*tajrī*) to a *mustaqarr* of its own. That is the taqdīr — the precise determination — of the Almighty, the All-Knowing."

The key word is **mustaqarr**, from the root meaning "to settle." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it can denote a *place* of rest or a *time* of rest — and can even mean the end-point of one journey where the next begins immediately, without any pause. The early authorities understood it in more than one way, and Ibn Kathir lays the views out:

**A destination in time.** Qatadah said it means "an appointed time and it will not go beyond that": the sun's flawlessly regular motion is not everlasting. It runs until the Day of Resurrection, when its course will be abolished, it will come to a halt and it will be rolled up. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supports this reading from Sūrah al-Zumar (39:5), where the sun and moon each run "for an appointed term" (*ajal musammā*), and notes that on this reading neither does the sense of the verse present any difficulty, nor does any objection of astronomy arise. A related view, narrated from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr, ties it to the sun's seasonal pattern — a summer course it does not exceed, then a winter course it does not exceed. Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās recited the phrase as *lā mustaqarra lahā* — "with **no** resting place" — meaning it never settles or slows, night or day, until the Resurrection, as in 14:33: the sun and moon "constantly pursuing their courses."

**A destination in place — beneath the Throne.** This rests on a hadith Ibn Kathir cites from Al-Bukhari, and which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes is reported in the Sahihs of al-Bukhari and Muslim and, apart from Ibn Majah, in all Six Books. Abu Dharr al-Ghifārī, may Allah be pleased with him, was with the Prophet ﷺ in the masjid at sunset. The Prophet ﷺ asked, "O Abu Dharr, do you know where the sun sets?" He replied, "Allah and His Messenger know best." The Prophet ﷺ said: "It goes and prostrates beneath the Throne — and that is what Allah says: *'And the sun runs on its fixed course for a term…'*" In another narration Abu Dharr asked about the verse directly and was told: "Its mustaqarr is beneath the Throne (*taḥt al-ʿArsh*)."

### The prostration of the sun

How does the sun "prostrate," and how does it go "beneath the Throne" when — as the Qurʼān and Sunnah themselves establish — the ʿArsh (the Throne of the Most Merciful) encompasses all the heavens and the earth, so that the sun is *always* beneath it? And since the sun is setting somewhere and rising somewhere else at every moment, with no pause in its motion, when would such a prostration occur? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes these questions seriously and gives the resolution of ʿAllāmah Shabbīr Ahmad ʿUthmānī, which it says finds support in the statements of several leading commentators.

First, a principle: the prophets build their proofs of Allah's existence, oneness, knowledge and power on what every human being can see — the prophetic teaching is synchronized with common perception, not with the technical apparatus of astronomers, because faith is the duty of the learned and unlettered alike. That is why, when people asked the Prophet ﷺ the secret behind the moon's waxing and waning, the Qurʼān answered on his behalf simply: "Say: they are indicative of time for the people, and of the Hajj" (2:189) — redirecting them from fruitless speculation to what actually serves them.

On that footing, the hadith opens up. The sun's *sajdah* is not the placing of a forehead on a floor; every created thing has a mode of worship suited to its nature — "everything already knows its ṣalāh and its tasbīḥ" (24:41). The sun's prostration *is* its perfect, unresisting submission: it moves only by Allah's permission and command, and since it is beneath the ʿArsh at all times and rising or setting somewhere at every moment, it is in a *perpetual* state of prostration throughout its orbit, seeking leave for every advance — with no pause needed. The Prophet ﷺ, standing with Abu Dharr at the charged moment of sunset, took that moment as suitable to teach the essential lesson: people should not take the sun to be an independent entity moving of its own volition and power. Every rising and every setting is by the permission and will of Allah. And the narrations add a solemn ending, in a hadith from ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿūd which Ibn Kathir transmits with reference to ʿAbd al-Razzāq: a day will come when the sun will not be given permission for the next circuit. It will be commanded to turn back and rise from the west — the sign that the Hour is absolutely close, after which the doors of īmān and repentance are closed and no declaration of faith or repentance will any longer be accepted.

Note the honesty of the classical tradition here: Ibn Kathir records his own understanding that the Throne is a dome above creation, and the sun nearest it at noon and furthest at midnight; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān registers the observational difficulties with taking the hadith that way and prefers ʿUthmānī's reading. The verse itself, Maʿārif insists, presents no difficulty on any reading — its point is untouched by any theory of Ptolemy or Pythagoras: **the sun neither came into existence by itself, nor moves by itself, nor sustains itself.** "That is the taqdīr of al-ʿAzīz" — a decree none can oppose or prevent, says Ibn Kathir — "al-ʿAlīm" — who knows every movement and every cessation of movement, and has set the whole in a pattern admitting no differences or inversions.

## Ayah 39 — the moon's stages and the old date-stalk

"And the moon — We have determined for it *manāzil*, until it returns like the *ʿurjūn qadīm*."

**Manāzil** (singular *manzil*) means the places one arrives at on a journey. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that Allah has bound the moon's movement to particular points; since it completes its circuit in a month, it has twenty-nine or thirty such stages, generally reckoned as twenty-eight because the moon disappears for at least a day each month. Ibn Kathir draws out the purpose: the moon runs a different orbit from the sun, *so that the months can be known from it just as day and night are known from the sun* — "They ask you about the crescent moons. Say: these are signs to mark fixed periods of time for mankind and for the Hajj" (2:189); "He made the sun a shining thing and the moon a light, and measured out for it stages that you might know the number of years and the reckoning" (10:5). The sun gives one constant kind of light and rules the day; the moon was decreed to change — and its changing is a calendar hung in the sky, readable by simple observation, which is exactly why the Sharīʿah tied the months, the fasting and the Hajj to the *sighting* of the new moon rather than to mathematical calculation.

Ibn Kathir traces the cycle as the eye sees it: the new moon rises small and faint; each night it climbs higher and brightens until the full moon of the fourteenth night; then it wanes until, at month's end, it "returns like the ʿurjūn qadīm" — **the old, dried stalk of the date-bunch**, which Ibn ʿAbbās identified as the original stem connecting the cluster of dates to the tree. When that stalk ages and dries, it bends like a bow — pale, curved, fine: the exact image of the dying crescent, drawn from the Arabs' own surroundings. Ibn Kathir even records how intimately the Arabs lived with this cycle: they had a name for every set of three nights in the month according to the moon's phases — from *Ghurar* at its start, through *al-Bīḍ*, "the white nights" of brilliant moonlight, to *Miḥāq*, named for the absence of moonlight.

## Ayah 40 — no collision, no confusion

"It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day; and each, in an orbit, is floating."

Two negations, then a summary of cosmic order. Mujahid explained: each of them has a limit it neither transgresses nor falls short of; when the time of one comes, the other goes away. ʿIkrimah put it concretely: each has its time when it prevails — so it is not appropriate for the sun to rise at night. The sun's authority is the day; the moon's authority is the night; neither trespasses on the other's domain. And "the night does not outstrip the day": after night has passed, another night cannot come until it has been day. Ad-Dahhak said, "The night does not depart from here until the day comes from here" — and he pointed to the east. Mujahid added, "they seek one another rapidly": there is no gap, no interval, because both have been subjugated and are constantly pursuing one another.

Then the closing phrase: *wa-kullun fī falakin yasbaḥūn*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that **falak** does not literally mean "sky" — it means the *orbit* in which a heavenly body moves; the verse thus indicates that the moon is not contained within some sky, as the astronomical theory of Ptolemy presumed, but moves in a particular orbit through space — something, Maʿārif observes, that recent investigation and even human travel to the moon have made certain. And *yasbaḥūn*: they are *floating* — revolving, as Ibn Kathir explains — night and day, sun and moon, each in its own orbit; this was the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Ad-Dahhak, Al-Hasan, Qatadah and ʿAtaʼ Al-Khurasani. Ibn ʿAbbās and others of the Salaf pictured it as "an orbit like the arc of a spinning wheel." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also draws a "special note" from these clarifications of the Qurʼān and hadith: the sun and the moon are both *in motion*, moving for a fixed term — refuting the presumption that the sun has no movement at all, an error the latest research has likewise refuted.

## What the signs are for

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān keeps returning to one discipline: the Qurʼān invites reflection on the heavens *to the extent that it serves faith and life*, and deliberately bypasses questions whose answers benefit no one in this world or the next — such as pinpointing where in eternity the sun's circuit began. The passage is not an astronomy lesson; it is an argument addressed to every observer of an ordinary sunset. Each of these ayat is an *āyah* — a sign — and the signs all point one way: the peeled-back day, the racing sun, the waning crescent and the seamless relay of night and day are not self-running machinery but subjugated servants, moving every moment under the permission and will of the Almighty, the All-Knowing. The believer who watches night fall is watching taqdīr in action — the sun receding not by its own power, but in obedience, seeking leave for every advance. And there is urgency folded into the sign: the narrations teach that the same sun which seeks permission for each circuit will one day be refused, be commanded to turn back and rise from the west — and at that hour the door of repentance will be closed, and no declaration of faith will any longer be accepted. The time to answer the signs is while they still shine.

passages.title: The laden ship: a sign of rescue and respite
passages.tafsir:
## The laden ship: a sign of rescue and respite

This passage sets before us one of the great signs (āyāt) of Allah's power and mercy: the ship. Coming after the signs already mentioned in the earth and the heavens, these four ayat turn to Allah's power over the sea — that He carries whole generations of humanity, with all their children and cargo, safely across deep water, when at any moment He could let the water take them. What holds the passage together is a single movement of thought: the gift (ayat 41–42), the ever-present danger behind the gift (ayah 43), and the mercy that alone keeps the danger at bay, for a while (ayah 44).

## The ship of Nuh, and every ship after it

In ayah 41, Allah says that He "bore their offspring in the laden ship" (al-fulk al-mashḥūn). Ibn Kathir explains that among the signs of Allah's might and power is that He has subjugated the sea to carry ships — and most significantly of all, the ship of Nuh, peace be upon him, in which Allah saved him and the believers, apart from whom none of the descendants of Adam were left on the face of the earth. Ad-Dahhak, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said explicitly, "This was the ship of Nuh, peace be upon him."

The word *mashḥūn* — "laden" — matters. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said, "Laden means filled," and this was also the view of Sa'id bin Jubayr, Ash-Sha'bi, Qatadah and As-Suddi. Ibn Kathir describes it as the ship filled with luggage and animals, in which Allah commanded Nuh to put two of every kind. The picture is not of a light vessel skimming the surface but of a heavily burdened one — and it is precisely the heavy, loaded ship staying afloat that the Qur'an presents as the wonder.

There is a subtlety in the wording of ayah 41 that the commentators draw out. Allah says He carried "their offspring" (*dhurriyyatahum*) — yet those who boarded were the people themselves. Ibn Kathir explains "their offspring" here as meaning their forefathers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers a complementary insight into why children are singled out: one's children and family place a great burden of responsibility on a parent, especially when they cannot move about on their own. The verse thus emphasises that the ship carried not only able-bodied adults but young children, the aged, and all their belongings — people and their things together. The mention of the most vulnerable passengers heightens the sense of what was at stake, and of what Allah preserved.

## "The like thereunto": what do they ride?

Ayah 42 — "And We have created for them of the like thereunto, on which they ride" — drew two readings from the early authorities, and both are recorded from Ibn 'Abbas himself.

**The camel.** Al-'Awfi narrates from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "This means the camel, for it is the ship of the land on which they carry goods and on which they ride." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Arabs naturally understood the verse this way, since the camel was their familiar carrier of heavy loads across countries — so much so that they themselves called the camel "the Boat of the Land."

**Later ships.** Ibn Jarir records that Ibn 'Abbas asked his companions whether they knew what this ayah refers to; when they said no, he said, "This refers to the ships which were made after the ship of Nuh, peace be upon him, which was similar to it." This was also the view of Abu Malik, Ad-Dahhak, Qatadah, Abu Salih and As-Suddi.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then makes a striking observation: it is obvious, the commentary says, that the Qur'an has not specifically named a camel or any other particular mode of conveyance at this place.
