The phrase *min mithlihi mā yarkabūn* — "things similar to it that they ride" — is left open, and so it embraces every means of transport that carries people and their baggage to their destination. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān even suggests that in our time the aeroplane has become the greatest substantiation of this Qur'anic statement: just as the ship sails on the surface of the water and the mass of water does not drown it, the aeroplane sails on the bed of air and the air does not let it fall. No wonder, the commentary adds, if the Qur'an left the wording open so that every mode of transport invented right up to the Day of Qiyamah would be included — and Allah knows best. The two early readings and this broader one are not rivals so much as widening circles of the same meaning.

## The danger held back only by mercy

Ayah 43 turns the sign over to show its other face: "If We will, We shall drown them, and there will be no shout for them, nor will they be saved." Ibn Kathir explains each phrase: those who would be drowned are the very people aboard the ships; "no shout for them" means there would be no one to save them from their predicament; "nor will they be saved" means no rescue from what has befallen them. The same sea that carries can swallow — and once it does, no cry for help avails and no rescuer comes. Safe passage is never a property of the ship itself; it is a permission renewed by Allah at every moment.

Then ayah 44 names the only exception: "Unless it be a mercy from Us, and as an enjoyment for a while." Ibn Kathir renders its sense: "but by Our mercy We make it easy for you to travel on land and sea, and We keep you safe until an appointed time." And the "while" — the *ḥīn* — is, as he says, "until a time that is known to Allah, may He be glorified and exalted." Two truths sit side by side in this ayah. First, every safe crossing, every journey completed, is not luck or engineering alone but *raḥmah* — mercy — from Allah. Second, even that mercy in this world is "enjoyment for a while": a respite with an appointed end known to Him. The passage thus closes the way it opened Nuh's story — with rescue — but reminds the reader that every rescue in this life is a loan of time, not an exemption from return to Allah.

## Living it

The passage asks for something simple and searching: to see one's own journeys — by sea, land, or air — as this ayah frames them. The believer who boards any vessel is re-enacting, in miniature, the situation of Nuh's passengers: carried over a depth that could claim them, held up by nothing but Allah's mercy, and granted enjoyment for a while, until a time known to Him. To travel with that awareness is to receive the sign the ayat were sent to point out.

passages.title: Refusing warnings, signs, and calls to give
passages.tafsir:
This short passage is a portrait of a heart that has sealed itself shut. Three doors are knocked on in turn — the door of warning (ayah 45), the door of signs (ayah 46), and the door of generosity (ayah 47) — and all three stay closed. What binds the ayat together is the repeated refrain *wa idhā qīla lahum*, "and when it is said to them": every time something is *said* to these people for their own good, the answer is either silence, aversion, or sarcasm.

## Where we are in the sūrah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. The verses just before these paraded the manifestations of Allah's power and wisdom — the heavens, the earth, the signs in creation — as an invitation to recognise the Creator and worship Him alone, with everlasting blessings promised for acceptance and severe punishment warned for rejection. Now the camera turns from the signs to the audience: the disbelieving people of Makkah, the direct addressees of this sūrah, who "remained unmoved and unaffected either when persuaded to do something reward-worthy, or when warned against some likely punishment." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that two dialogues between the believers and the disbelievers are narrated here — one about fearing Allah's punishment (ayah 45), and one about feeding the poor (ayah 47).

## Ayah 45 — a warning met with silence

"Beware of what is before you and what is behind you, so that you may receive mercy." What exactly is "before" them and "behind" them? Ibn Kathir records more than one reading. Mujahid said the phrase refers to their sins; others, Ibn Kathir notes, said it is the opposite — reading the two directions the other way around. Ibn Kathir's own framing gathers both ends of the span: the idolators persisted in their misguidance, paying no attention either to the sins they had committed in the past or to what was to come upon them in the future, on the Day of Resurrection. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the same span in terms of punishment: the believers were urging them to fear a punishment of Allah that can arrive *before* them even in this world, and that must in any case meet them in the Hereafter after death.

Notice the gentleness of the invitation itself. The warning ends with *laʿallakum turḥamūn* — "so that you may receive mercy." Ibn Kathir explains: if you fear these things, Allah will have mercy on you and save you from His punishment. Even the threat is wrapped in an offer of mercy. The call is not "fear, so that you may be crushed" but "fear, so that you may be spared."

**The missing answer.** Here the passage does something remarkable with grammar, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out beautifully. Ayah 45 sets up a condition — "and when it is said to them…" — but the Qur'an never states what they did in reply. In the terminology of Arabic syntax, the apodosis (the "then…" clause that should complete the "when…" sentence) is deliberately elided, left unspoken. Why? Because the next ayah supplies it: their settled habit of *iʿrāḍ* — aversion, turning away — from every sign proves what their response to this warning must have been too. This is why translations add words like "still they turn away" or "they pay no heed" in brackets: the Qur'an lets their notorious track record speak, rather than dignifying their silence with a report. Their non-response is itself the response. Ibn Kathir makes the same observation from the other side: the wording implies that they would not respond, but would turn away and ignore it.

## Ayah 46 — no sign ever landed

"Whenever a sign comes to them from their Lord, they turn away from it." Ibn Kathir explains that "sign" (āyah) here means the signs of Tawhid — the oneness of Allah — and the truth of the Messengers. And "turn away from it" means "they did not accept it or benefit from it." That second phrase is worth sitting with: the failure is not merely that they rejected the signs outright, but that even the signs that reached them produced no benefit in them. The verse is total in its sweep — *never* did a sign come *except* that they turned away. Not one exception in the record. This is the settled disposition that made the elided answer of ayah 45 unnecessary to state.

## Ayah 47 — the theology of stinginess

The third door is the call to give: "Spend from what Allah has provided you." Ibn Kathir specifies the scene: the disbelievers are being told to spend on the poor and needy among the Muslims. Notice how the very wording of the appeal already contains its own argument — *mimmā razaqakum Allāh*, "from what *Allah* has provided *you*." The wealth in their hands is itself Allah's gift; they are only being asked to pass a portion of it on.

Their reply is the most articulate rejection in the passage — and the most revealing: "Shall we feed those whom, if Allah willed, He would have fed? You are only in plain error."

Ibn Kathir unpacks the logic: 'those you tell us to spend on — if Allah had wanted, He would have made them independent and fed them from His own provision; so by withholding, we are simply in accordance with the will of Allah concerning them.' And "you are only in plain error" means: in error *by telling us to do that*.

**Why the argument is upside-down.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān exposes the sarcasm at the heart of this reply. These same Makkans, it points out, themselves confessed that Allah is the Provider — the Qur'an elsewhere records that if you asked them who sends down water from the sky and revives the dead earth with it, "they will certainly say, 'Allah'" (al-ʿAnkabūt 29:63). So they were not making a sincere theological objection; they were pressing into service a truth they already accepted. "When Allah is the Razzāq, the Provider, let Him provide for them too — why should we?" As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, these people spoke as if giving to the poor were somehow *contrary* to Allah's attribute of being the Master-Provider of all sustenance.

**How Allah actually provides.** This is where Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the passage's deepest teaching: the wisdom behind some people receiving their sustenance *indirectly*. Allah is perfectly capable of delivering everyone's provision personally and directly — and with the animals and insects, He does exactly that. In that kingdom there is no rich and no poor; no one gives to anyone; "everyone dines from nature's own food spread." Human beings are deliberately different. Allah gives to one person and makes him a *conduit* — a channel of delivery — for others, so that He gives to the poor *through* the rich. The purposes are named: to make human social life just, to cultivate the spirit of mutual help and cooperation, so that the one who spends earns reward and the one who receives becomes grateful.

And beneath that lies a still sharper observation: the whole functioning order of the world runs on mutual need. The poor person needs the rich person's money; the rich person needs the poor person's labour. Neither is free of the other — and so, on reflection, "nobody is doing a favor to anybody." Whatever a person gives, he gives, in the final analysis, in his own interest and for his own good. The disbelievers' sneer — "shall *we* feed them?" — imagined charity as a one-way favour they were being conned into. On Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's account, the giver is in fact a conduit in Allah's own arrangement of provision, and the giving works, in the ultimate analysis, to the giver's own good.

**A subtle juristic point.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also addresses a question a careful reader might raise: on what basis did the believers call *disbelievers* to spend in Allah's way at all, when — as the jurists maintain — disbelievers are not addressees of the subsidiary injunctions of the Sharīʿah (the detailed practical rulings, as opposed to the fundamental call to faith)? The answer: the believers were not asking them to implement a religious injunction. They appealed to them on the basis of the accepted norms of human goodwill, sympathy, and gentleness — the common decency any human being can be called to. What the disbelievers turned down, then, was not a demand of religious law but an appeal to ordinary human sympathy.

## Reading the three ayat as one

Set side by side, the three refusals form a complete anatomy of a closed heart. Warned about the consequences of sin in this world and the next — no reply worth recording (ayah 45). Shown sign after sign of Allah's oneness and the truth of His Messengers — habitual turning away (ayah 46). Asked to do the simplest human good, feed the hungry — a sarcastic argument that turns Allah's own lordship into an excuse for tight-fistedness, and brands the callers as the ones in "plain error" (ayah 47). The progression matters: fear did not move them, evidence did not move them, and compassion did not move them. And the passage's final irony is left ringing: the people who accused the believers of *ḍalāl mubīn*, plain error, were — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes — the ones who "just did not understand" how Allah's provision actually operates in the world.

For the believer, the passage carries a quiet warning of its own. The claim "if Allah willed, He would have fed them" is still heard today in subtler dress — every argument that treats another's need as Allah's problem rather than my summons. On the teaching Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from these verses, the fact that Allah could feed the poor directly and has instead placed provision in *your* hand is no excuse to withhold: you were made the conduit. The reward of the spender and the gratitude of the receiver are both part of what Allah, al-Razzāq, is providing.

passages.title: The mocked Hour answered: Blast, Trumpet, and Judgment
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the Qur'an's answer to a sneer. The Makkans had been mocking the believers with the question, "When will this threat come to pass?" — and in seven swift ayat Allah replies not with a date but with a scene: one Blast that freezes the world mid-argument, the Trumpet blast that empties the graves, the cry of the risen deniers, and the calm verdict of a Day on which no soul is wronged. What holds ayat 48–54 together is a single movement from mockery to reality — the question asked in scorn (ayah 48) is answered by the very Hour it scorned (ayat 49–54).

## The question that was never a question

**Ayah 48** quotes the disbelievers: *"When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?"* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is emphatic about what kind of question this was: it was asked "by way of mockery, and the real purpose was to deny the Day of Judgment. It was not asked for finding out the truth." It was a taunt aimed at the Muslims. Ibn Kathir reads it the same way — the disbelievers thought the Resurrection would never come to pass, and he links their demand to Allah's words elsewhere: *"Those who believe not therein seek to hasten it"* (42:18).

Maʿārif adds two further points worth sitting with. First, even if the question had been sincere, the mercy of the Lord requires that the precise year and day of the Hour be given to no one — not even to any of His noble prophets and messengers. Second, the question is absurd on its own terms: a reasonable person who learns that something is certainly coming starts preparing for it; he does not waste his time demanding its exact hour. The mockers had heard the warning of Qiyāmah; sense demanded that they believe and work for success in the life to come. Instead, says Maʿārif, they were so entangled in heedlessness that they were virtually waiting for the Day itself to arrive before they would think about it.

This is also why the passage begins where it does. Maʿārif notes that the preceding verses had recorded dialogues between believers and disbelievers — the believers urging them to fear Allah's punishment and to spend on the poor, the disbelievers answering with aversion and sarcasm. Ayah 48 is the climax of that aversion: having brushed aside every sign, they now dare the punishment to come.

## One Blast, mid-sentence — ayat 49–50

So Allah answers: *"They await only but a single Ṣayḥah which will seize them while they are disputing"* (ayah 49). The **Ṣayḥah** is a single overwhelming Blast or Cry — one, not a series; no warning shots. And the detail that carries the whole scene is the phrase *"while they are disputing."* Life will not pause respectfully for the end of the world. Ibn Kathir explains — adding, in his careful way, "and Allah knows best" — that this is the trumpet blast of terror: the Trumpet will be blown while people are in their marketplaces and places of work, arguing and disputing as they usually do. In that state Allah will command Isrāfīl to blow into the Trumpet, and he will sound a long note; no one will be left on the face of the earth but will tilt his head to listen to the sound coming from heaven. Then those still alive will be driven to the gathering place by a fire surrounding them on every side.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a hadith that makes the suddenness almost photographic: two men will be engaged in buying and selling cloth, the yardage stretched out between them, when the Hour comes — and they will never complete the deal; another man will be plastering his water tank and will fall dead in that very state (reported by Abu Nuʿaym from Sayyidna Abu Hurairah, as quoted by al-Qurtubi).

**Ayah 50** presses the point home: *"Then they will not be able to make bequest, nor will they return to their family."* Ibn Kathir observes that they will be unable to make a bequest regarding their possessions "because the matter is more serious than that" — the last worldly duty a dying person performs, and there will be no time even for it. Maʿārif adds the mirror image: those caught away from home will not have the respite even to step inside their own houses. People will lie dead in exactly the state the Blast found them. Maʿārif identifies this as the first blowing of the Horn (ṣūr), by which the entire order of the heavens and the earth is destroyed; Ibn Kathir describes the fuller sequence — after this blast of terror comes the blast at which everyone alive dies, besides the One Who is Ever-Living, Eternal, and after that the trumpet blast of the resurrection is sounded.

## The graves empty — ayah 51

*"And the Trumpet will be blown, and behold, from the graves they will come out quickly to their Lord."* Ibn Kathir identifies this as the trumpet blast of the resurrection, and — counting by the fuller sequence he has just described (the blast of terror, then the blast at which everyone alive dies, then the raising of the dead) — he calls it "the third blast of the trumpet." The scholars' ways of numbering the blasts differ in their details: the translation of this ayah glosses it as the Trumpet blown "a second time," and the report of Qatādah cited under the next ayah likewise speaks of "the two trumpet blasts," while Ibn Kathir's own scheme counts three. What every account agrees on is what this blast does: the graves open, and the dead rise.

Two Arabic words in this ayah repay attention. **Ajdāth** is the plural of *jadath*, a grave. **Yansilūn**, from *nasalān*, means to walk swiftly — the risen do not trudge; they rush. Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif both connect it to the parallel verse: *"The Day when they will come out of the graves quickly, as racing to a goal"* (70:43).

Maʿārif also resolves an apparent tension with 39:68, where the risen are described as standing and looking around: there is no contradiction — first comes the instant of standing up in wonder, then the racing toward the plains of the Resurrection. And since the Qur'an establishes that the angels will summon people to that plain, the disbelievers' arrival will be no act of willingness; the call of the angels will compel them to come hastening.

## "Who has raised us from our sleeping place?" — ayah 52

Now the mockers speak again — but the tone has changed entirely. *"Woe to us! Who has raised us up from our place of sleep (marqad)?"* This is the same crowd that asked "when?" in ayah 48; confronted with the answer, their taunt collapses into a wail.

But why do they call the grave a "place of sleep," when the Qur'an and Sunnah affirm punishment in the grave? Ibn Kathir addresses this directly: there is no contradiction, "because in comparison to what is to come afterwards, that will seem like a nap." Maʿārif says the same — the disbelievers were already in punishment in their graves with no relief, yet next to the horrors of Qiyāmah it will seem as nothing, so they will cry out that it would have been better to have stayed where they were. Ibn Kathir also records another explanation from the early authorities: Ubayy bin Kaʿb (may Allah be pleased with him), Mujāhid, Al-Ḥasan, and Qatādah said, "They will sleep before the Resurrection," and Qatādah specified that this will be between the two trumpet blasts.

The answer comes at once: *"This is what the Most Gracious (al-Raḥmān) had promised, and the Messengers spoke truth!"* Who says it? Ibn Kathir reports that more than one of the Salaf held it will be the believers who respond; Al-Ḥasan said the angels will reply — and, Ibn Kathir concludes, there is no contradiction because both are possible, and Allah knows best.

Maʿārif pauses on the choice of name. Of all Allah's attributes, why **al-Raḥmān** — the Most Merciful — at this terrifying moment? Maʿārif explains that the name serves as an indicator: in His mercy, Allah had already made elaborate arrangements for them to remain safe from this very punishment, and His alerting them in advance — through His promise, His Books, and His Prophets — was itself a dictate of His attribute of mercy.

## One command, perfect justice — ayat 53–54

**Ayah 53** returns to the note on which the scene opened: *"It will be but a single Ṣayḥah, so behold, they will all be brought up before Us."* One Blast ended the world; one Blast assembles all of humanity for judgment. Ibn Kathir gathers the parallel verses: *"But it will be only a single Zajrah, when behold, they find themselves alive on the surface of the earth"* (79:13–14); *"And the matter of the Hour is not but as a twinkling of the eye, or even nearer"* (16:77); and 17:52. His summary of the meaning: "We will issue but one command, and all of them will be gathered together."

And then, after all the terror, **ayah 54** closes the passage on justice: *"This Day, no soul will be wronged in anything, nor will you be requited except for what you used to do."* Ibn Kathir's gloss is brief because the ayah is plain: none will be wronged with regard to his deeds; the only currency of that Day is what a person actually did. The mockers demanded a date; what they are given instead is a guarantee — the Day will come without appointment, and when it comes, the accounting will be exact.

## Living it

The passage's own logic supplies its lesson, and Maʿārif states it outright: once you know a thing is certainly coming, the reasonable response is preparation, not calendar-questions. Every detail here — the unfinished cloth deal, the will that cannot be made, the family that cannot be reached — teaches that the door of action is open only now, mid-transaction, mid-dispute, mid-ordinary-day. And ayah 54 tells the believer exactly what to carry to that Day: nothing will count against you unjustly, and nothing will count for you except what you used to do.

passages.title: The joys of the people of Paradise
passages.tafsir:
# The Joys of the People of Paradise (36:55–58)

After having mentioned the worries of the people of Jahannam, the sūrah turns the page completely. Ayat 55–58 describe the state of the people of Paradise on the Day of Qiyāmah — enjoying themselves. The four ayat unfold in sequence: activity (55), companionship and rest (56), provision (57), and finally the greeting of Peace from the Lord, Most Merciful (58).

## Ayah 55: Joy as an occupation

The passage opens: *"Indeed, on that Day the residents of Paradise will be busy enjoying."* Ibn Kathir explains that when the people of Paradise have reached the arena of judgement and settled in the gardens, they will be too preoccupied with their own victory and their new life of eternal delights to worry about anyone else. Al-Hasan al-Basri and Ismāʿīl bin Abī Khālid said they will be too busy to think about the torment the people of Hell are suffering. Mujāhid — a view shared by Qatādah — said their "busyness" is with the delights they are enjoying, and Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, said simply: they will be rejoicing.

The wording repays attention. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *fākihūn* (the plural of *fākih*) signifies happiness of the heart together with happiness drawn from one's surroundings — inner joy matched by an environment of joy. And the phrase *fī shughul*, "in occupation," does real work here. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two readings. One, echoing the commentators above: they will be totally unaffected by the misfortunes afflicting the people of Jahannam. The other answers a question a thoughtful reader might quietly ask: in Jannah there will be no religious duty like obligatory worship and no job of earning one's livelihood — would such a lack of activity leave one uptight or bored? The ayah forestalls the thought: their enjoyment itself will be their principal activity, and the question of any boredom simply does not arise.

## Ayah 56: Companionship, shade, and rest

*"They and their spouses will be in shade, reclining on thrones."* The joy of Paradise is not solitary. Mujāhid explained *azwājuhum* as their spouses, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the word here includes both the ḥūrs of Jannah and the wives of the mortal world.

The "shade" (*ẓilāl*), Mujāhid said, is the shade of trees. As for *al-arāʾik*, rendered "thrones," a remarkable roll-call of early authorities — Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Muhammad bin Kaʿb, Al-Hasan, Qatādah, As-Suddī and Khusayf — all explained it as beds beneath canopies. The picture, then, is not of stiff royal seats but of canopied beds, upon which the people of Paradise recline.

## Ayah 57: Whatever they call for will come

*"There they will have fruits and whatever they desire."* Ibn Kathir's comment on the fruits is brief and sweeping: fruits "of all kinds"; and "whatever they ask for, they will find it, all kinds and types."

But the finest point in this ayah is a single word choice, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out beautifully. The Qur'an says *mā yaddaʿūn* — a derivation from *daʿwā*, "to call" — whatever the people of Jannah call for or wish to have will come to them. It deliberately does not say *yasʾalūn*, "they ask." Why? Because having something after having asked for it is itself a sort of exertion, and Jannah will be free even of that. It will be a place where everything needed is already ready and present.

## Ayah 58: "Peace" — a word from the Lord, Most Merciful

The passage has moved through activity, companionship, and provision, and closes not with a thing but with a word: *"Salām" — a word from a Lord Most Merciful.*

Ibn Kathir relates, through Ibn Jurayj, the explanation of Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him: Allah Himself — Who is As-Salām, the Peace — will grant peace to the people of Paradise. Ibn Kathir notes that this view of Ibn ʿAbbās is like another ayah: *"Their greeting on the Day they shall meet Him will be 'Salām'"* (33:44).

## Reading the passage whole

Taken together, the four ayat give a complete portrait of the people of Paradise on that Day: joy within the heart and in the surroundings (*fākihūn*); enjoyment so absorbing that — as Al-Hasan al-Basri said — they will be too busy even to think of the torment of the people of Hell; spouses beside them in the shade of trees, reclining on canopied beds; fruits of all kinds, with whatever they call for coming to them before the exertion of asking; and, crowning it all, *Salām* — peace granted by Allah Himself, a word from a Lord Most Merciful.

passages.title: The criminals separated and sentenced to Hell
passages.tafsir:
# The Criminals Separated and Sentenced (36:59–64)

This passage takes us to a single, terrible scene on the Day of Resurrection: the moment the guilty are ordered out of the ranks of humanity, confronted with the covenant they broke, and shown the Fire they were warned about all their lives. What binds these six ayat together is that they are one continuous divine address — Allah Himself speaking to the criminals, first commanding them to separate (ayah 59), then rebuking them with three piercing questions (ayat 60–62), and finally pronouncing the sentence (ayat 63–64).

## The great separation — ayah 59

"Step away, you criminals" (*wa-mtāzū l-yawma ayyuhā l-mujrimūn*). Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us the end of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, when He commands them to get apart from the believers — to stand as a distinct, exposed group.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān paints the sequence vividly. When people first rise from their graves, they will be scattered and mixed together — the Qurʼān elsewhere describes them "as if they are scattered locusts" (al-Qamar 54:7). But then, group by group, they will be sorted according to their deeds: disbelievers in one place and believers in another, sinners in one place and the righteous and accepted in another — as at-Takwīr 81:7 says, "when the persons will be divided into pairs." Ayah 59 is the moment that sorting is announced: the mixed crowd of the resurrection is divided, and the mixing ends.

Ibn Kathir shows that this separation is a theme the Qurʼān returns to again and again: "Stop at your place! You and your partners… Then We shall separate them" (10:28); "on the Day when the Hour will be established — that Day shall they be separated" (30:14); "On that Day they shall be divided" (30:43) — meaning, he says, divided into two separate groups; and the command to the angels, "Assemble those who did wrong, together with their companions and what they used to worship instead of Allah, and lead them on to the way of flaming Fire" (37:22–23).

## The rebuke: "Did I not command you?" — ayat 60–62

What follows is not a request for information but a rebuke — Ibn Kathir calls it exactly that: a rebuke from Allah to the disbelievers among the sons of Adam, who obeyed Shayṭān even though he was a plain enemy to them, and disobeyed ar-Raḥmān — the Most Merciful — Who created them and granted them provision. The contrast is the sting of the ayah: they abandoned the One who gave them everything for the one sworn to destroy them.

Ayah 60 uses the language of a covenant: "Did I not command you (*a-lam aʿhad ilaykum*), O Children of Adam, that you should not worship Shayṭān? Verily, he is a plain enemy to you." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this address on the Day of Qiyāmah is directed to all human beings — even, it adds, to the jinn.

**How did they "worship" Shayṭān?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious objection: the disbelievers did not generally bow down to Shayṭān; they worshipped idols and other things. So how does this charge fall on them? The answer given is a definition worth holding onto: to submit to some entity in the absolute sense — to obey it in word and deed, in everything and under all conditions — is nothing but worship. Because these people always followed Shayṭān's teachings, they were rightly called his worshippers. In support of this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a saying it attributes to hadith — without naming which collection records it — that a person who, driven by love of money or spouse, does whatever will increase his wealth or please his spouse even at the cost of Allah's displeasure, is "the obedient servant of the silver coin" and "the obedient servant of the spouse" (*ʿabd ud-dirham*, *ʿabd uz-zawjah*). Worship, in other words, is measured by whom you actually obey when obedience costs you — not by what you formally bow to.

**"And that you should worship Me — that is the straight path" (ayah 61).** Ibn Kathir unfolds the meaning as Allah's own reminder of what was demanded in the world: 'I commanded you to disobey Shayṭān, and I commanded you to worship Me, and this is the straight path — but you followed a different path and you followed the commands of Shayṭān.' The "straight path" (*ṣirāṭ mustaqīm*) is named right there in the ayah: worshipping Allah alone.

**"He led astray a great multitude of you" (ayah 62).** The unusual word *jibillan* means a large number of people — Ibn Kathir records this as the view of Mujāhid, Qatādah, as-Suddī and Sufyān bin ʿUyaynah. Shayṭān's success was not marginal; whole multitudes followed him. And then the question that closes the rebuke: "Did you not then understand?" (*a-fa-lam takūnū taʿqilūn*). Ibn Kathir renders its force: did you have no understanding at all, when you went against the command of your Lord to worship Him alone, with no partner or associate, and preferred to follow Shayṭān? The charge is not merely disobedience but irrationality — the enemy was *plain*, openly declared, and they served him anyway.

## The sentence — ayat 63–64

Then the scene shifts from words to sight. Ibn Kathir says that on the Day of Resurrection this will be said to the disbelievers *after Hell has been shown to them*, as a rebuke and a warning: "This is Hell which you were promised!" (ayah 63) — meaning, 'this is what the Messengers warned you about, and you did not believe them.'

"Burn therein this Day, for that you used to disbelieve" (ayah 64). The sentence names its own cause: *bimā kuntum takfurūn* — because of your disbelief. Ibn Kathir sets beside it the parallel scene in sūrah aṭ-Ṭūr: "The Day when they will be pushed down by force to the fire of Hell, with a horrible, forceful pushing. This is the Fire which you used to belie. Is this magic, or do you not see?" (52:13–15). There, too, the deniers stand before the very Fire they used to call a lie, and the questions put to them leave no room for denial.

The passage does not end the exchange here. Ibn Kathir notes that in the ayat that follow, the mouths of these same deniers will be sealed and their own hands and legs made to testify to what they used to earn — their denial will not even survive their own bodies.

## Living it

The passage's definition of worship is its most searching gift to a living reader. No one consciously sets out to "worship Shayṭān"; the criminals of ayah 59 certainly did not think of themselves that way. Yet the Qurʼān names absolute obedience — following an authority in everything, even against Allah — as worship of that authority. The saying of the "servant of the dirham" cited by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān extends the diagnosis to money and even to family: whatever you will not disobey for Allah's sake has become, functionally, your object of worship.

And the question of ayah 62 — "Did you not then understand?" — implies that avoiding this fate is within the reach of ordinary understanding. The enmity of Shayṭān is *plain* (ayah 60); the alternative is stated in one clause (ayah 61): worship Allah alone — that is the straight path. The separation of ayah 59 happens on the Last Day, but which side of it a person stands on is being decided in the choices of obedience made now.

passages.title: Sealed mouths, testifying limbs, and Allah's power over bodies
passages.tafsir:
# The Body as Witness: Ayat 65–68

This passage takes us inside the courtroom of the Day of Resurrection — and then turns the lens back on us in this world. In ayah 65 Allah describes what He **will** do on that Day: seal the mouths of the deniers and let their own limbs testify against them. In ayat 66–67 He tells us what He **could have done, had He willed**: wiped out their eyes or transformed them where they stood. And in ayah 68 He points to what He **already does** before everyone's eyes: reversing the strong human frame back into weakness through old age. What binds the four ayat together is a single theme — your body belongs to Allah, not to you. It will obey Him against you on the Day of Judgment, its sight and movement continue only because He has not willed otherwise, and its slow unwinding in old age is a proof of resurrection displayed in every household.

## Ayah 65: The sealed mouth and the speaking hands

Why would mouths need to be sealed? Because, as Ibn Kathir explains, this is the state of the disbelievers and hypocrites when they stand before Allah: they will **deny the sins they committed** in this world and swear that they never did them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the scene from the Qur'an itself: the mushriks — those who ascribed partners to Allah — will actually take an oath before their Lord, "By Allah, our Lord, we ascribed no partners to Allah" (al-Anʿām 6:23), and some will insist the angels wrote things in their record that they never did.

At that moment the lying tongue is simply switched off. Allah sets a seal on their mouths — *nakhtimu ʿalā afwāhihim* — and transfers the power of speech to the very hands that earned the deeds and the legs that walked to them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes them as court witnesses: the criminal is silenced, and the evidence speaks for itself.

**Reconciling the verses about testifying limbs.** A careful reader may notice that different ayat name different witnesses. Here it is the hands and legs; in Sūrah Fussilat (41:20) it is "their ears and their eyes and their skins"; and in Sūrat al-Nūr (24:24) even "their tongues will testify against them." Does a testifying tongue contradict a sealed mouth? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers: no — the "seal" means the person can no longer say anything *by his own choice*. The tongue itself, like the other limbs, will then speak against its owner's will and testify to the truth.

**How can a hand speak?** The Qur'an has already answered this, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, in Sūrah Fussilat: when the people ask their own skins, "Why did you testify against us?", the limbs reply that Allah, "who has given power of speech to all things endowed with the ability to speak" (41:21), has made them speak too. The One who gave the tongue its speech in the first place can give it to any part of His creation.

## From the Sunnah: the servant who argues with his Lord

Ibn Kathir preserves a remarkable report that turns this ayah into a full scene. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Anas bin Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "We were with the Prophet ﷺ and he smiled so broadly that his molar could be seen," then he ﷺ asked, "Do you know why I am smiling?" The companions replied, "Allah and His Messenger know best." He ﷺ then described how a servant will argue with his Lord on the Day of Resurrection. The servant will say, "O Lord, will You not protect me from injustice?" Allah will say, "Of course." The man will then insist, "I will not accept any witness against me except from myself." Allah will reply, "Today you will be a sufficient witness against yourself, and the honorable scribes will serve as witnesses against you." His mouth will then be sealed and his faculties commanded: "Speak!" — and they will speak of everything he did. When he is finally allowed to speak again, he will turn on his own limbs and cry, "May you be doomed! It was for you that I was fighting." Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith was also recorded by Muslim and An-Nasa'i.

Notice the bitter irony the hadith exposes: everything the man sinned for — the appetites and advantage of that very body — becomes the prosecution's star witness. He demanded a witness "from myself," and Allah, who never wrongs anyone, granted exactly that.

Ibn Kathir also cites a report narrated by Ibn Jarir from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari, may Allah be pleased with him, which sets the two possible endings side by side. The **believer** will be shown his deeds privately, just between him and his Lord. He will admit them — "Yes, O Lord, I did do that" — and Allah will forgive his sins and conceal them so that no creature on earth sees them, while his good deeds are displayed for all to see. The **disbeliever and hypocrite**, by contrast, will deny: "O Lord, by Your glory, this angel has written down things that I did not do." When the angel confronts him with the time and place and he still swears his denial, Allah seals his mouth. Abu Musa then offered his own supposition — "I think that the first part of his body to speak will be his right thigh" — and recited this very ayah. The lesson is piercing: it is not the sin alone but the *denial* that brings the seal. Honest admission before Allah is met with forgiveness and concealment; brazen denial is met with the body's own testimony.

## Ayat 66–67: "Had We willed…" — the power held back

The passage now pivots with two conditional sentences: *wa-law nashāʾu* — "and if We willed."

**Ayah 66 — the wiped-out eyes.** "Had We willed, We would surely have wiped out their eyes, so that they would struggle for the path — how then would they see?" Ibn Kathir records that the early authorities understood this in two complementary ways, both traced to Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him. On one occasion he explained it literally: "We could have blinded them" — and al-Hasan al-Basri pictured it: Allah could have covered their eyes and made them blind, stumbling about. On another occasion Ibn ʿAbbās gave the deeper reading: "If We willed, We could have misguided them all away from true guidance, so how could they be guided?" — physical sight standing for spiritual sight. Mujahid, Abu Salih, Qatadah and as-Suddi explained "the path" as the right way, and Ibn Zayd said the path here means *the truth*: how could they see it if Allah covered their eyes? Al-ʿAwfi reports Ibn ʿAbbās summing up "how then would they see?" as: "They would not see the truth." The two readings converge on one point — both eyesight and insight are gifts held in Allah's hand.

**Ayah 67 — transformed where they stand.** "Had We willed, We could have transformed them in their places." The word rendered "transformed" (from *masakhnāhum*) drew a range of explanations from the Salaf, which Ibn Kathir lists: Ibn ʿAbbās (in al-ʿAwfi's report) said "We could have destroyed them"; as-Suddi, "We could have changed their form"; Abu Salih, "We could have turned them to stone"; al-Hasan al-Basri and Qatadah, "We could have caused them to sit on their feet." Different wordings, one threat: whatever the exact form, the result is what the ayah itself states — "then they would have been unable to go forward, nor could they have turned back." Ibn Kathir spells it out: unable to move to the front, unable to move backwards — they would have remained static, unable to move forwards or backwards.

## Ayah 68: The proof written into old age

Then comes the turn that makes the threat undeniable: "And whomever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation. Will they not then understand?" You might doubt an unseen Day when limbs will testify — but you cannot doubt what happens to every human body given enough years.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the two key words. *Nuʿammirhu* ("We give him long life") comes from *taʿmīr*, prolonging the years of life. *Nunakkishu* comes from *tankīs* — to reverse, invert, turn upside down. Allah describes aging not as mere decline but as a **reversal**. Ibn Kathir connects it to the ayah "Allah is He Who created you in weakness, then gave you strength after weakness, then after strength gave weakness and gray hair" (30:54), and to "among you there is he who is brought back to the miserable old age, so that he knows nothing after having known" (22:5).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces the whole arc: a lifeless drop, wrapped in layers of darkness in the mother's womb; the infusion of the spirit; the infant nourished at the mother's breast; the climb through stages to a body in full bloom — and then, when the Creator decides, the same strengths waning stage by stage until the old man has, in effect, returned to his childhood: habits change, hearing fades, sight dims, what was once comfort becomes suffering. The commentary even quotes the poet al-Mutanabbi: for one who lives long in the world, it turns upside down before his eyes until what he saw as truth starts appearing to be a lie.

Ibn Kathir draws out the intended conclusion: this world is transient and will come to an end; it is not eternal. "Will they not then understand?" means — will they not think about how they were created, then turn gray, then grow old and senile, and realize from this that they were created *for another world*, one that does not pass away: the Hereafter?

And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a final, tender observation: even this reversal is a mercy. All our strengths are functional devices issued on loan, never our property, and they must be taken back. Allah could reclaim them all at once — but the Most Merciful takes them back gradually, in long, spaced-out installments, precisely so that a person is alerted in time and starts preparing for the ultimate journey of the Hereafter.

## Living this passage

The passage leaves the believer with two clear postures. First, honesty before Allah now and on that Day: Abu Musa's report shows that the one who admits his sins finds forgiveness and concealment, while the one who denies is silenced and testified against by his own limbs. Second, attentiveness to the body's sermon: every gray hair and weakened joint is *tankīs* — a scheduled reminder that these limbs are on loan, that they will one day speak, and that their gradual return to weakness is Allah's kindness, giving us time to make ready before the seal is set.

passages.title: The Quran is revelation, not poetry
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

Ayat 69–70 answer, once and for all, the slander that the Qur'an was poetry and the Prophet ﷺ a poet. Allah declares that He never taught His Messenger poetry — indeed it would not even befit him — and then states what the Qur'an actually is: "a Reminder and a plain Qur'an" (ayah 69), sent "to warn whoever is truly alive, and that the Word may be justified against the disbelievers" (ayah 70). The two ayat hold together as denial and affirmation: first the false label is stripped away, then the true purpose is announced.

## Why they called it poetry

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the background. The deniers of the Prophet's ﷺ mission could not deny the one thing that was a matter of common experience: the unique effectiveness of the Qur'an, its ability to move hearts. So they invented convenient excuses. At times they called this Divine Word magic and the Prophet ﷺ a magician; at other times they said it was poetry and he a poet. The aim of both labels was the same — to explain away the Qur'an's power over hearts as something other than what it was. If it was sorcery, its impression on hearts was a spell; if it was poetry, well, poetic speech also moves people. Either way, they could avoid the conclusion that this was the speech of Allah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then raises the obvious objection: how could this charge ever have been made? The Arabs were a people with poetry in their blood — even their women and children composed impromptu lines. They knew exactly what poetry was: bound by meter, by *radīf* (the unchanging word at the end of a hemistich) and *qāfiyah* (the changing rhyme-word before it). The Qur'an is restricted by none of these. Not even someone pathetically ignorant of the conventions of poetry would think of calling it poetry.

Two answers are given. First, at its essence "poetry" for them meant self-structured imaginary subjects — whether cast in verse or in prose. By calling the Qur'an poetry, they meant: what you have brought is no more than imaginary tales. Second, they may have used the word because of a perceived congruity of effect — the Qur'an stirred hearts the way great poetic composition stirred hearts, so they filed it under the only category they had for such speech.

## "We have not taught him poetry, nor is it fitting for him"

Ayah 69 refutes both the claim and its very possibility. Ibn Kathir explains that "nor is it suitable for him" means the Prophet ﷺ did not know how to compose poetry, did not like it, and had no natural inclination towards it. It was narrated that he never memorized a stanza of poetry with its correct meter or rhyme — he would transpose the words or remember it incompletely.

Ibn Kathir cites an example recorded by Al-Bayhaqi in *Ad-Dala'il*: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ once quoted back to the poet Al-'Abbas bin Mirdas As-Sulami, may Allah be pleased with him, his own line — "Do you distribute my booty and the booty of the servants between Al-Aqra' and 'Uyainah?" — but with the two names reversed, breaking the verse. Al-'Abbas corrected him: "It is 'Uyainah and Al-Aqra'." The Prophet ﷺ replied, "It is all the same" — the meaning is identical. His ear simply did not bend to meter.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a second incident, reported by Imam Abu Bakr al-Jassas with his own chain of authority: Sayyidah 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, was asked whether the Prophet ﷺ ever recited poetry. She said no — except that he once recited a verse of Ibn Tarfah, "The time will reveal to you that which you did not know, and the news will be brought to you by one whom you did not appoint to do so" — but he recited it in a way that broke the poetic measure. Sayyidna Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, pointed out, "Ya RasulAllah, this verse is not like that." He answered, "I am not a poet, nor is poetry appropriate for me." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Ibn Kathir reports this narration in his Tafsir, and that at-Tirmidhi, an-Nasa'i and Imam Ahmad have also reported it.

Ibn Kathir draws the two threads together: the Prophet ﷺ was both naturally disinclined to compose verse and forbidden to do so by Divine Law. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, he did not even consider reciting other people's poetry as appropriate for himself — that he would compose it was unthinkable. And if a sentence of his occasionally happened to fall into poetic rhythm, it was casual, not intended composition; one or two accidental metrical lines do not make a person a poet.

One caution from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: this special condition of the Prophet ﷺ, which rested on great considerations of wisdom, does not mean poetry is blameworthy in any absolute sense — that ruling is treated in detail under Surah Ash-Shu'ara' (26:224) in that commentary.

## "This is only a Reminder and a plain Qur'an"

Having removed the false label, ayah 69 gives the true one: *dhikr* — a Reminder — and *qur'ānun mubīn* — a plain, clear Qur'an. Ibn Kathir explains "plain" as clear and self-explanatory to the one who ponders and comprehends its meanings. And its origin is not human craft at all: Allah taught him the Qur'an, of which He says, "Falsehood cannot come to it from before it or behind it; sent down by the All-Wise, Worthy of all praise" (41:42). It is not poetry as some of the ignorant disbelievers of Quraysh claimed, nor sorcery, fabrication, or a magic spell, as the misguided variously suggested.

## Ayah 70: a warning for the living, a case closed against deniers

Ayah 70 states why this plain Qur'an was sent: "to warn whoever is truly alive, and that the Word may be justified against the disbelievers." Ibn Kathir explains the first clause: the Qur'an warns every living person on the face of the earth — like the ayat "that I may therewith warn you and whomsoever it may reach" (6:19) and "but those of the sects that reject it, the Fire will be their promised meeting place" (11:17).

But there is a deeper layer in "whoever is alive." Ibn Kathir says that those who actually benefit from the warning are those whose hearts are alive and who have enlightened insight. Qatadah said: "Alive of heart and alive of insight." Ad-Dahhak said: "This means wise."

The second clause completes the picture. "That the Word may be justified against the disbelievers" means, as Ibn Kathir puts it, that the Qur'an is a mercy to the believers and evidence against the disbelievers. The same revelation divides its hearers: for the living heart it is warning and mercy; for the one who rejects it, it becomes evidence against him.

## Taking it to heart

The passage asks the reader a searching question: which of the two receptions describes you? The Qur'an's power to move hearts was undeniable even to its enemies — their problem was not evidence but the labels they invented to escape it. The believer's task is the opposite: to come to this "plain Qur'an" as one who ponders and comprehends its meanings, with a heart that is — in Qatadah's words — alive and possessed of insight, so that the Reminder lands as mercy and not as evidence.

passages.title: Cattle as blessings, yet they worship helpless idols
passages.tafsir:
This passage sets two pictures side by side and asks the reader to feel the absurdity of the contrast. On one side: cattle — living, powerful creatures that Allah alone created, then handed over to human beings as property, transport, food, and drink. On the other: idols — objects that cannot help their worshippers, cannot help themselves, and will one day stand as evidence against the very people who served them. The hinge between the two halves is the question at the end of ayah 73: *"Will they not then be grateful?"* Everything before it is the case for gratitude; everything after it is what ingratitude actually looks like.

## The case for gratitude: a gift no one earned

The passage opens (ayah 71) with a striking phrase: *"Do they not see that We have created for them, of what Our Hands have fashioned, the cattle…"* We affirm this attribute as it comes, in the way befitting Allah's majesty — without likening it to creation and without explaining it away. The point the ayah presses is exclusivity: as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, man played no role whatsoever in the creation of these animals. Allah made them, so to speak, exclusively by His own hand — and then did something more. He did not merely let people benefit from the cattle; He made them their *owners* (mālikūn), free to use them, or sell them and use the money.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a far-reaching lesson from this. Modern economic theories argue over what justifies ownership — the capitalist says capital and wealth, the socialist says labor. This ayah, he says, cuts underneath both: neither capital nor labor creates anything. Creation is Allah's act directly, and reason demands that the one who creates a thing is its true owner. So the essential, real ownership of everything belongs to Allah; human ownership takes effect only when Allah, in His mercy, passes it on — and He has revealed through His prophets the law by which ownership is proven and transferred. Ownership, in other words, is not a human achievement but a divine grant.

The gift then deepens: *"And We have subdued them unto them"* (ayah 72). Both commentaries linger here, because the fact is so familiar we stop seeing it. A camel, a horse, an ox, an elephant — each is far stronger than a man. By any natural reckoning, humans should never have been able to tame them. Ibn Kathir, citing Qatadah's gloss that "they are their masters," paints the scene: a young child can walk up to a camel, make it kneel, make it stand, and drive it — and even if the caravan runs to a hundred camels or more, that one child could lead them all. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same image with a horse: a boy takes the reins of a powerful animal and rides it wherever he pleases. This docility is not human cleverness. Allah built subservience into these free creatures' natures — a grace, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, given to man without his even asking.

From there the ayat itemize what the cattle provide, and Ibn Kathir unpacks each phrase as the inventory runs on into ayah 73. Riding: mounts for journeys and beasts to carry burdens to every region. Eating: their meat, when people choose to slaughter and sacrifice them. "Other benefits": wool, fur, and hair, from which come furnishings and articles of comfort. "Drinks": their milk — and Ibn Kathir adds even their urine, for those who need it as medicine. Nothing about the animal is wasted; every part of it serves.

Then comes the question that turns the whole inventory into an argument: *"Will they not then be grateful?"* Ibn Kathir spells out what gratitude means here — not merely a feeling of thankfulness, but worship: will they not worship the One who created and subdued all of this, without directing their gratitude to others? In the Qurʼān's logic, shukr (gratitude) paid to anyone other than the Giver is not gratitude at all.

## The turn: helpless gods

Ayah 74 delivers the indictment. Despite all this, *"they have taken besides Allah gods, hoping that they might be helped."* Ibn Kathir explains the idolaters' hope: that these gods would help them, provide for them, and bring them closer to Allah. Ayah 75 demolishes the hope in one line: *"They cannot help them."* Those idols cannot aid their worshippers — they are too weak, too insignificant, too powerless. They cannot even help *themselves* or take revenge on anyone who wants to harm them, because they are inanimate objects that neither hear nor comprehend. The contrast with the first half of the passage is the whole point: Allah gives living, breathing, useful blessings; the false gods cannot lift a finger even in their own defense.

The second half of ayah 75 — *"and they are for them a troop brought forward (jund muḥḍarūn)"* — carried two interpretations among the early scholars, and the sources present both.

**The view of Mujahid:** this refers to the Day of Reckoning. The idols will be gathered and made present when their worshippers are brought to account — adding to the worshippers' grief and making the proof against them all the more decisive. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same sense: the very things they worshipped will turn against them on the Day of Judgment and bear witness against them. The "troop" turns out to be an army for the prosecution.

**The view of Qatadah and al-Hasan al-Basri:** the irony plays out already in this world. The idolaters used to get angry for the sake of their gods, yet those gods could bring them no benefit and ward off no harm — they were mere idols. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing al-Qurtubi's report of this tafsir, sharpens the reversal: people took idols as gods hoping the idols would help *them*, but in reality the worshippers ended up as the idols' servants and soldiers — standing guard over them, taking their side, and fighting anyone who opposed them. The relationship of help flows entirely the wrong way. Ibn Kathir calls this a good opinion and notes it was the view favored by Ibn Jarir, may Allah have mercy on him.

The two readings are not really rivals: in this world the worshippers serve their helpless gods, and in the next those same gods are marched out as evidence against them.

## Consolation for the Prophet ﷺ

The passage closes (ayah 76) by turning to the Messenger ﷺ himself: *"So let not their speech grieve you. Verily, We know what they conceal and what they reveal."* Ibn Kathir — under a heading he calls "Consolation for the Mercy to the Worlds" — explains "their speech" as their denial of the Prophet ﷺ and their disbelief in Allah. The comfort offered is Allah's complete knowledge: He knows everything about them, open and hidden, and will deal with them accordingly on the Day when no deed, great or small, major or minor, will be overlooked — when everything they did in their worldly lives is laid open for examination. The Prophet ﷺ is not asked to answer every taunt; the reckoning rests with the One from whom nothing is hidden.

## Living it

The passage's demand on the reader is contained in that one question in ayah 73: *afalā yashkurūn* — will they not be grateful? Every ordinary comfort listed here — the riding, the meat, the milk, the wool, fur, and hair that become furnishings and articles of comfort — is a created gift from a Creator who owed us none of it, and whom we did nothing to earn it from. Gratitude, in this passage's terms, means recognizing the true Owner behind everything we "own" and directing worship to Him alone — because the alternative the passage shows us is a person pouring devotion into something that cannot help him, and finding on the Day of Judgment that his god has become a witness against him.

passages.title: From sperm-drop to resurrection: 'Be,' and it is
passages.tafsir:
This closing passage of Sūrah Yā Sīn answers the oldest objection to the resurrection — "who could revive rotten bones?" — with a single sustained argument: the One who made you from a drop of fluid, who strikes fire from green wood, and who built the heavens and the earth, needs only to say **"Be!"** and it is. The seven ayat move from man's smallest beginning (a sperm-drop) to the largest things in existence (the heavens and the earth), and end where the whole sūrah has been heading: everything returns to Him.

## The bone in his hand

Ibn Kathir records that these final verses of Yā Sīn came down over a real confrontation in Makkah. According to Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, ʿUrwah bin Az-Zubayr, As-Suddi and Qatādah, it was Ubayy bin Khalaf who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ holding a dry bone, crumbling it and scattering the dust into the air: "O Muhammad! Are you claiming that Allah will resurrect *this*?" The Prophet ﷺ answered: "Yes — Allah, may He be exalted, will cause you to die, then He will resurrect you and will gather you into the Fire." Then these ayat, to the end of the sūrah, were revealed.

A second report, recorded by Ibn Abi Hātim from Ibn ʿAbbās (and by Ibn Jarīr from Saʿīd bin Jubayr), names Al-ʿĀs bin Wā'il, who picked a bone from a valley bed, crushed it in his hand, and asked, "Will Allah bring this back to life after it has disintegrated?" The Prophet's ﷺ reply carried the same import: "Yes, Allah will cause you to die, then He will bring you back to life, then He will make you enter Hell." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes there is nothing improbable in the event having happened with both men. And Ibn Kathir adds the point that matters most for the reader: whichever man it was, the wording of ayah 77 — *al-insān*, "man" with the generic definite article — deliberately widens the address to **every** denier of the resurrection, in every age. The scene is ancient; the question is permanent.

## Forgetting your own creation

The Qur'an's first move is not to look outward but to turn the objector's gaze back on himself. In ayah 77, Allah reminds man that He created him from a *nuṭfah* — a sperm-drop, which Ibn Kathir describes as something "insignificant, weak and despised," citing the parallel ayat "Did We not create you from a despised water?" (77:20–22) and "Verily, We have created man from Nuṭfah" (76:2), a mixture of fluids. Yet from that lowly origin, "behold, he stands forth as an open opponent" — *khaṣīm mubīn*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the bitter irony: a creature made from a lowly drop now has the audacity to challenge his Maker and deny His power.

Ayah 78 names the precise failure: "he puts forth for Us a parable **and forgets his own creation**." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that as the man ground the bone to powder and declared its revival impossible, he forgot the far stranger example he himself embodies — life infused into a lowly, lifeless drop. Had he remembered his own origin, he would never have dared say "no" to divine power. Ibn Kathir puts it the same way: man knows, just by looking at himself, that Allah has already done something *greater* than the thing he calls impossible — He brought him into existence from nothing.

So ayah 79 gives the Prophet ﷺ his answer, and it is devastatingly simple: "Say: He will give life to them Who created them the first time — and He is the All-Knower of every creation." Ibn Kathir highlights that second clause: the objection "the bones are scattered" assumes Allah could lose track of them. But He knows every bone in every region of the earth — where each fragment went when it disintegrated and dispersed. Re-creation poses no problem to One whose knowledge encompasses every particle.

**Two hadith from the sources bring this home.** Imam Ahmad records in his Musnad, from Bishr bin Jahhāsh, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ one day spat in his hand, placed his finger on it, and conveyed Allah's words: "Son of Adam, how can you outrun Me when I have created you from something like this? And when I have fashioned you and formed you, you walk in your cloak on the earth... You accumulate and do not spend until the death rattle reaches your throat, then you say, 'I want to give in charity' — but it is too late for charity." (Also recorded by Ibn Mājah.)

And Imam Ahmad records, from Ribʿi, that ʿUqbah bin ʿAmr asked Hudhayfah to relate what he had heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Hudhayfah told of a man who, when death approached and all hope of life was gone, instructed his family: gather a great pile of firewood, set it ablaze until my flesh is consumed and my bones become brittle, then take them, grind them, and scatter them in the sea. They did so — but Allah gathered him together and asked him, "Why did you do that?" He said, "Because I feared You." So Allah forgave him. ʿUqbah added that he too had heard the Prophet ﷺ say this, and that the man was a gravedigger.

Ibn Kathir notes that many versions of this hadith were recorded in the Two Sahihs. One of those versions relates that the man commanded his sons to burn him, grind his remains into small pieces, and scatter half of them on land and half on the sea on a windy day. They did so; then Allah commanded the sea to gather whatever remains were in it, and commanded the land to do likewise, then said to him, **"Be!" — and he was a man, standing.** Allah asked him, "What made you do what you did?" He said, "The fear of You, and You know best" — and straight away He forgave him. The story is almost a live demonstration of ayat 78–79: scattering the bones changes nothing — and in that version, the restoring word is the very *kun* ("Be!") of ayah 82.

## Fire from a green tree

Ayah 80 adds a proof the Makkan audience could touch: "He Who produces for you fire out of the green tree, when behold, you kindle therewith." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Qurtubi) and Ibn Kathir (in a view reported from Ibn ʿAbbās) explain that two trees of the Hijaz, the *Markh* and the *ʿAfār*, were famous for exactly this: a traveller with no kindling would cut two green twigs — solid, moist, full of fresh water inside — rub one against the other, and fire would spring out, as from a firestone.

Why is this an argument for resurrection? Qatādah states it plainly: "The One who brought forth this fire from this tree is able to resurrect him." Fire and wet greenness are opposites; life and dry bones are opposites. The One who draws flame out of dripping wood every day in front of you can draw life out of dust. Ibn Kathir adds a second layer: Allah first made the tree itself *from water*, made it green and fruitful, then turned it into dry firewood — He transforms His creation from state to state as He wills, "and none can stop Him." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that on this wider reading every tree qualifies — green today, fuel tomorrow, as in 56:71–72 — though the word *akhḍar* ("green") suggests the specific fire-bearing trees are primarily meant.

## The greater creation, and the word "Be"

Ayah 81 raises the argument to its largest scale: "Is not He Who created the heavens and the earth able to create the like of them?" Ibn Kathir explains: the seven heavens with their stars and planets, the seven earths with their mountains, sands, oceans and wildernesses — if He made *these* without difficulty, recreating human bodies is the lesser task, as Allah says elsewhere, "The creation of the heavens and the earth is indeed greater than the creation of mankind" (40:57). Ibn Jarīr links it to 46:33: He "was not wearied by their creation." The ayah answers its own question — *balā*, "Yes, indeed!" — and seals it with two names: **al-Khallāq al-ʿAlīm**, the Supreme Creator, the All-Knowing. Power and knowledge together: He can remake you, and He knows exactly how and from where.

Then ayah 82 reveals *how* Allah creates: "His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, 'Be!' — and it is" (*kun fa-yakūn*). Ibn Kathir: He commands a thing **once**; the command needs no repetition and no confirmation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds this beautifully: Allah has no need of the human way of making things — gathering raw materials, assembling workers, labouring over time. His way is a single word. And Maʿārif adds a subtle point: this does not mean everything must appear instantly. When His wisdom decrees instant creation, it is instant; when His wisdom decrees gradual creation, it unfolds gradually — either built into the first decree or by a fresh *kun* at each stage. The gradualness of nature is not a limit on His power; it is His power operating on His own chosen schedule.

Imam Ahmad records from Abu Dharr that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ conveyed Allah's own commentary on this ayah: "O My servants, all of you are sinners apart from those whom I protect... Seek My forgiveness and I will forgive you... **My giving is a word and My punishment is a word. When I want a thing to happen I merely say to it 'Be!' and it is.**" The same word that will raise the dead is the word by which He forgives and provides — which is why the hadith frames omnipotence as an invitation to seek His forgiveness, not merely a threat.

## Glory, dominion, and the return

Ayah 83 closes the sūrah in praise: "So glorified be He in Whose Hand is the *malakūt* of all things, and to Him you shall be returned." *Malakūt* means dominion or sovereignty. Ibn Kathir notes a difference of opinion: some claimed *al-mulk* refers to the physical realm and *al-malakūt* to the spiritual realm, but the majority of the scholars of Tafsir hold — and Ibn Kathir prefers — that the two words mean the same thing: total dominion. Glorified, exalted and sanctified above any evil, Ibn Kathir writes, is the Ever Living, the Self-Sufficient, in Whose Hand is the control of the heavens and the earth; His is the power to create and command; and to Him all mankind returns on the Day of Resurrection, when He will reward or punish each according to his deeds, "and He is the Just, the Generous Bestower."

This word *malakūt* lived in the Prophet's ﷺ own worship. Imam Ahmad records from Hudhayfah bin Al-Yamān that in a night prayer in which the Prophet ﷺ recited the seven long sūrahs in seven rakʿahs, he said after rising from bowing: "Praise be to Allah, the Owner of Malakūt, might, pride and greatness." And Abu Dawud records from ʿAwf bin Mālik Al-Ashjaʿī a night prayer in which the Prophet ﷺ recited Al-Baqarah — pausing at every mercy-ayah to ask for mercy, and at every punishment-ayah to seek refuge — then said in his bowing: "Glory be to Allah, the Owner of might, Malakūt, pride and greatness" (also recorded by At-Tirmidhi in Ash-Shamā'il and An-Nasā'i). The sūrah's final ayah is not only doctrine; it is the vocabulary of prostration.

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with three things. First, an answer to carry: whenever the resurrection seems far-fetched — to a questioner or to your own heart — the reply is the one Allah taught His Prophet ﷺ in ayah 79: the One who made you the *first* time will make you the second time, and He has lost track of nothing. Second, a way of seeing: your own body, and something as ordinary as striking a fire, are standing proofs of the power you are asked to trust. Third, an urgency drawn from the hadith of Bishr bin Jahhāsh: do not hoard and withhold until the death rattle, when it is "too late for charity." The sūrah ends with the certainty *"to Him you shall be returned"* — and the wise response is to give, seek forgiveness, and glorify the Owner of the dominion of all things before that return arrives.
